Subir Sachdev

Abstract

Two of the iconic phases of the hole-doped cuprate materials are the intermediate temperature pseudogap metal and the lower temperature dd-wave superconductor. Following the prescient suggestion of P. W. Anderson, there were numerous early theories of these phases as doped quantum spin liquids. However, these theories have had difficulties with two prominent observations:
(i) angle-dependent magnetoresistance measurements (ADMR) in the pseudogap metal, including observation of the Yamaji effect, present convincing evidence of small hole pockets which can tunnel coherently between square lattice layers (Fang et al., Nature Physics 18, 558 (2022); Chan et al., Nature Physics 21, 1753 (2025)) and
(ii) the velocities of the nodal Bogoliubov quasiparticles in the dd-wave superconductor are highly anisotropic, with vF≫v�v_{F}\gg v_{\Delta} (Chiao et al., Phys. Rev. B 62, 3554 (2000)).
 
These lecture notes review how the fractionalized Fermi Liquid (FL*) state, which dopes quantum spin liquids with gauge-neutral electron-like quasiparticles, resolves both difficulties. Theories of insulating quantum spin liquids employing fractionalization of the electron spin into bosonic or fermionic partons are discussed. Doping the bosonic parton theory leads to a holon metal theory: while not appropriate for the cuprate pseudogap, this theory is argued to apply to ultracold atom experiments on the Lieb lattice. Doping the fermionic parton theory leads to a dd-wave superconductor with nearly isotropic quasiparticle velocities. The construction of the FL* state in a single band Hubbard-type model is described using a quantum dimer model, followed by a more realistic description using the Ancilla Layer Model (ALM), which is then used to obtain the theory of the pseudogap and the dd-wave superconductor. The ALM also leads to a variational wavefunction for the FL* state of the Hubbard model, and its local correlations agree well with ultracold atom observations.

1 Introduction

These lectures begin by presenting the conventional Hartree-Fock theory of antiferromagnetic order in the square lattice Hubbard model in Section 2. The state with antiferromagnetic order is generically a metal, with electron and/or hole pocket Fermi surfaces. However, precisely at half-filling, and only if the antiferromagnetic order is large enough, the Fermi surfaces disappear, and we obtain an insulating antiferromagnet.

Sections 3 and 4 present the theory of insulating quantum spin liquids in two spatial dimensions, involving many-boson (i.e. spin) entanglement. These are states at half-filling which are insulating without any antiferromagnetic order or other broken symmetry. No such states appear in the theory of Section 2, or in other conventional approaches found in condensed matter texts published before the 1980s. We describe these states by the powerful parton method, which requires the presence of emergent gauge fields. Section 3 expresses the electron spin operator in terms of bosonic partons, while Section 4 employs fermionic partons.

The bosonic parton theory on triangular lattice leads to the theory of the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [1, 2, 3]. This is the simplest quantum spin liquid which can have time-reversal symmetry, and its spectrum of fractionalized ‘anyon’ excitations is the same as that of the toric code [4].

The bosonic parton theory on the square lattice leads to a U(1) gauge theory which maps at low energy to the C​P1\mdmathbb{CP}^{1} field theory, along with additional Berry phases for Dirac monopole configurations in the U(1) gauge field [5, 6] (Section 3.5). This theory describes the transition from the antiferromagnetically ordered Néel state to a valence bond solid (VBS), with a gapless spin liquid regime between them.

The fermionic parton theory on the square lattice is discussed in Section 4. Its low energy theory is a SU(2) gauge theory with 2 flavors (Nf=2N_{f}=2) of massless Dirac spinons [7, 8, 9, 10]. Remarkably this SU(2) gauge theory has a duality mapping [11] to the U(1) gauge theory of bosonic partons in Section 3.5.

The remaining sections involve entangled states with mobile many-fermion entanglement. The greater complexity of many-fermion entanglemet has also been explored in some recent mathematical papers [12, 13].

Section 5 moves the bosonic parton theory of Section 3 away from half-filling. This leads a ‘holon metal’ state, which is relevant for the Hubbard model on the Lieb lattice, as realized in ultracold atom experiments [14, 15]. But holons cannot tunnel coherently between square lattice layers, and so we argue that ADMR experiments [16, 17] imply that the holon metal cannot describe the cuprate pseudogap metal.

Section 6 examines charge fluctuations in the fermionic parton theory of Section 3 at half-filling. As the charger gap is reduced, we obtain a dd-wave superconductor and also a variety of competing charge-order states. But the dd-wave superconductor has nearly isotropic velocities for the Bogoliubov quasiparticles, in contrast to observations [18].

The Fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*) state [19, 20] is introduced in Section 7. The theory of FL* in a single-band Hubbard-type model is developed, and argued to resolve the problems with applications to the cuprates noted above. The FL* state does not obey the conventional Luttinger constraint on the size of the Fermi surface: in Section 7.1, we discuss generalized Luttinger constraints which are obeyed by FL* and other fractionalized states. The half-filled charge fluctuation theory of Section 6 is extended to non-zero doping in this framework.

The concluding Section 8 discusses the implication of the FL* theory of the pseudogap metal for the rest of the cuprate phase diagram.

2 Spin density wave order in the Hubbard model

We consider the onset of magnetism at a non-zero wavevector in a metal, often called a spin density wave (SDW). We will focus on the case where the wavevector of the SDW is 𝑲=(�,�){\bm{K}}=(\pi,\pi) on the square lattice, and so the ordering has the same symmetry as the Néel state in an insulating antiferromagnet. The main ingredient here will be a bosonic collective mode representing antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations in the metal: this boson is the ‘paramagnon’.

2.1 Fermi surface reconstruction

Let us now move into the antiferromagnetic metal phase, where we assume there is a 𝑷{\bm{P}} condensate at wavevector 𝑲=(�,�){\bm{K}}=(\pi,\pi)

⟨𝑷𝒊⟩=�𝒊​𝒩​𝒛^,\left\langle{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{i}}}\right\rangle=\eta_{{\bm{i}}}\,\mathcal{N}\hat{\bm{z}}\,, (10)

where the factor

�𝒊=±1\eta_{{\bm{i}}}=\pm 1 (11)

on the two checkerboard sublattices of the square lattice, and 𝒩\mathcal{N} measuring the strength of the Néel ordered moment shown in Fig. 2.

We wish to describe the excitations of this state. One class of excitations are spin waves: these can be obtained by considering transverse fluctuations of 𝑷{\bm{P}} about the condensate in (10) using the full action in (5). However, there are also low energy fermionic excitations in the antiferromagnetic metal, which are gapped in the insulator. We can determine the spectrum of the fermions by inserting (10) into the Yukawa coupling; using �𝒊=ei​𝑲⋅𝒓𝒊\eta_{{\bm{i}}}=e^{i{\bm{K}}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{{\bm{i}}}}, with 𝑲=(�,�){\bm{K}}=(\pi,\pi), we can write the fermion Hamiltonian in momentum space

�=𝒩.\Delta=\mathcal{N}\,. (13)

To obtain the fermionic excitation spectrum, we have to perform the analog of the Bogoliubov rotation in BCS theory. This is achieved by writing HAFMH_{\rm AFM} in a 2×22\times 2 matrix form by using the fact that 2​𝑲2{\bm{K}} is a reciprocal lattice vector, and so "𝒌+2​𝑲="𝒌\varepsilon_{{\bm{k}}+2{\bm{K}}}=\varepsilon_{{\bm{k}}}; correspondingly, the prime over the summation indicates that it only extends over half the Brillouin zone of the underlying lattice, shown in the left panel of Fig. 4, which is the Brillouin zone of the lattice with Néel order.

(14)

It is now easy to diagonalize the 2×22\times 2 matrix in (14), and we obtain

E𝒌±="𝒌+"𝒌+𝑲2±[("𝒌−"𝒌+𝑲2)2+�2]1/2E_{{\bm{k}}\pm}=\frac{\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}+\varepsilon_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{K}}}}{2}\pm\left[\left(\frac{\varepsilon_{\bm{k}}-\varepsilon_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{K}}}}{2}\right)^{2}+\Delta^{2}\right]^{1/2} (15)

The spectrum in (15) is not gapped, or even positive definite. Rather, it is the spectrum of a metal, in which the negative energy states are filled, and bounded by a Fermi surface. For small �\Delta, the structure of the Fermi surface can be deduced from the pictorial argument in Fig. 3: gaps open at the ‘hotspots’ where both "𝒌\varepsilon_{\bm{k}} and "𝒌+𝑲\varepsilon_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{K}}} vanish, reconstructing the large Fermi surface into small pockets. The Fermi surfaces so obtained is shown in Figs. 4, 5, 6 for different values of the electron density 1−p1-p. Here pp is conventionally the hole doping, and electron doping corresponds to p<0p<0. The dispersion "𝒌\varepsilon_{\bm{k}} has hoppings t1,2,3t_{1,2,3} to first, second, and third neighbors with t1,3>0t_{1,3}>0 and t2<0t_{2}<0 as appropriate for the cuprates.

We observe that the ‘large’ Fermi surface of the paramagnetic metal has ‘reconstructed’ into small pocket Fermi surfaces in the SDW state. The excitations of the SDW metal are hole-like quasiparticles on the Fermi surfaces surrounding the hole pockets, and electron-like quasiparticles on the Fermi surfaces surrounding the electron pockets. The spin wave excitations interact rather weakly with the fermionic quasiparticle excitations: this can be see from a somewhat involved computation from the effective action.

Finally, we discuss the fate of the Luttinger relation in this metal. The Luttinger relation connects the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface to the density of electrons, modulo 2 electrons per unit cell. It should be applied in the Brillouin zone of the Néel state, which is half the size of the Brillouin zone of the underlying square lattice, as shown in Fig. 4. In real space, this corresponds to the fact that the unit cell has doubled, and so the density of electrons per unit cell is 2​(1−p)2(1-p). For spinful electrons, the Luttinger relations measures electron density modulo 2, and so the density appearing in the Luttinger relation is −2​p-2p. This has to be equated to twice the volumes enclosed by the electron and hole pockets within the diamond shaped Brillouin zone in Fig. 4. Let 𝒜h\mathcal{A}_{h} be the area of a single elliptical hole pocket: there are 4 such pockets in the complete Brillouin zone of the square lattice or 2 pockets in the Brillouin zone of the Néel state, as is apparent from Figs. 4, 5, 6. Similarly, let 𝒜e\mathcal{A}_{e} be the area of a single elliptical electron pocket: there are 2 such pockets in the complete Brillouin zone of the square lattice or 1 pocket in the Brillouin zone of the Néel state. These arguments show that the Luttinger relation becomes

2×1(2​�)2/2×(−2​𝒜h+𝒜e)=−2​p.2\times\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2}/2}\times\left(-2\mathcal{A}_{h}+\mathcal{A}_{e}\right)=-2p\,. (16)

On the left hand side, the first factor is the spin degeneracy, and the second factor is the inverse of the volume of the Brillouin zone of the Néel state. To reiterate, this is the conventional Luttinger relation applied after accounting for the doubling of the unit cell, and it determines a linear constraint on the areas of the electron and hole pockets.

Fig 7 shows the electron spectral density (as measured by photoemission) at zero frequency for both the electron and hole pockets. This is computed by taking the imaginary part of the Green’s function (!−HAFM+i​�)−1(\omega-H_{\rm AFM}+i\eta)^{-1} of the matrix Hamiltonian in Eq. (14), where �\eta is a positive infinitesimal.

3 Bosonic spinon theory of quantum spin liquids

Section 2 has obtained an insulator at p=0p=0 with Néel order 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Decreasing 𝒩\mathcal{N} eventually leads to a metallic state with 𝒩=0\mathcal{N}=0, even at p=0p=0. But there was no insulator at p=0p=0 with no broken symmetry, and no such insulator is possible within the conventional Hartree-Fock framework. In this section we show that an insulator can indeed be obtained at p=0p=0 without any broken symmetry, but only after introducing fractionalized spin excitations.

As long as the charge gap is finite, we can perform a canonical transformation of the Hubbard model in Eq. (1) to spin-only Heisenberg antiferromagnet

ℋJ=∑𝒊<𝒋J𝒊​𝒋​𝑺𝒊⋅𝑺𝒋.{\cal H}_{J}=\sum_{{\bm{i}}<{\bm{j}}}J_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\,{\bm{S}}_{\bm{i}}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{\bm{j}}\,. (17)

The J𝒊​𝒋J_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} are short-ranged antiferromagnetic exchange interactions between S=1/2S=1/2 spins 𝑺𝒊{\bm{S}}_{\bm{i}} on sites 𝒊{\bm{i}}. We will consider here the square and triangular lattices with nearest neighbor interactions, but the methods generalize to a wide class of lattices and interaction ranges. Our analysis will be carried out for the nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian, and we will search for mean-field theories without any broken symmetries. In practice, we know that the nearest neighbor models on both the square and triangular lattices have antiferromagnetic order. But the strategy here is to understand the general structure of the spin liquid states, which can then be realized in more general Hamiltonians.

In this section, we employ a method which fractionalizes the spin operator into bosonic partons. On the square lattice, this leads to the low energy U(1) gauge theory with complex scalars in Eq. (94), and to the phase diagram in Fig. 17. This phase diagram is in good agreement with numerical studies [21, 22, 23] of the square lattice antiferromagnet with first and second neighbor exchange (the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model), and also of Sandvik’s JJ-QQ model [24].

Section 4 fractionalizes the spin operator into fermionic partons. This leads ultimately to a seemingly different low energy theory on the square lattice: a SU(2) gauge theory with massless Dirac fermions in Eq. (4.1), which initially did not agree with numerical studies of square lattice antiferromagnets. Wang et al. [11] argued that the bosonic and fermionic theories are equivalent, and that the confining phases of the SU(2) gauge theory lead to the same phase diagram as the bosonic partons. This equivalence is powerful, as it yields a toolbox of different approaches to study the square lattice spin liquid. In particular, upon including charge fluctuations, it is the fermionic parton theory that allows study of the confining instability of the square lattice spin liquid to dd-wave superconductivity that we study in Sections 6 and 7.7.

In the bosonic parton approach, we introduce the Schwinger boson description [25], in terms of elementary S=1/2S=1/2 bosons. For the group SU(2) the complete set of (2​S+1)(2S+1) states on site 𝒊{\bm{i}} are represented as follows

|S,m⟩≡1(S+m)!​(S−m)!(b𝒊↑†)S+m(b𝒊↓†)S−m|0⟩,|S,m\rangle\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{(S+m)!(S-m)!}}(b_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger})^{S+m}(b_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger})^{S-m}|0\rangle, (18)

where m=−S,…​Sm=-S,\ldots S is the zz component of the spin (2​m2m is an integer). We have introduced two flavors of Schwinger bosons on each site, created by the canonical operator b𝒊​�†b_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}, with �=↑,↓\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow, and |0⟩|0\rangle is the vacuum with no Schwinger bosons. The total number of Schwinger bosons, nbn_{b}, is the same for all the states; therefore

This procedure is similar to that employed in deriving the Landau-Ginzburg theory of superconductivity from electron pairing, with the crucial difference that now the Lagrangian ℒJ{\cal L}_{J} has a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge invariance associated with the local constraint in Eq. (19):

These saddle-point equations have been solved for the square and triangular lattices with nearest neighbor exchange JJ, and they lead to stable and translationally invariant solutions for �¯𝒊\bar{\lambda}_{{\bm{i}}} and 𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}. The only saddle-point quantity which does not have the full symmetry of the lattice is the orientation of the 𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}. Note that although it appears that such a choice of orientation appears to break inversion or reflection symmetries, such symmetries are actually preserved: the 𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} are not gauge-invariant, and all gauge-invariant observables do preserve all symmetries of the underlying Hamiltonian. For the square lattice, we have �¯𝒊=�¯\bar{\lambda}_{{\bm{i}}}=\bar{\lambda}, 𝒬¯𝒊,𝒊+x^=𝒬¯𝒊,𝒊+y^=𝒬¯\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{x}}=\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{y}}=\bar{\mathcal{Q}}. Similarly, on the triangular lattice we have 𝒬¯𝒊,𝒊+e^p=𝒬¯\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{e}_{p}}=\bar{\mathcal{Q}} for p=1,2,3p=1,2,3, where the unit vectors

e^2\displaystyle\hat{e}_{2} =\displaystyle= (1/2,−3/2)\displaystyle(1/2,-\sqrt{3}/2)
e^3\displaystyle\hat{e}_{3} =\displaystyle= (−1,0)\displaystyle(-1,0) (33)

point between nearest neighbor sites of the triangular lattice. We sketch the orientation of the 𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} on the triangular lattice in Fig. 8.

We can also compute the dispersion !𝒌\omega_{\bm{k}} of the k excitations. These are fractionalized bosonic particles which carry spin S=1/2S=1/2 and charge 0, named ‘spinons’. They should be contrasted from the spin-wave excitations of ordered magnets, which carry integer spin and charge 0. Their dispersion on the square lattice is

!𝒌=(�¯2−J2​𝒬¯2​(sin⁡kx+sin⁡ky)2)1/2\omega_{\bm{k}}=\left(\bar{\lambda}^{2}-J^{2}\bar{\mathcal{Q}}^{2}(\sin k_{x}+\sin k_{y})^{2}\right)^{1/2} (34)

while that on the triangular lattice is [3]

with kp=𝒌⋅e^pk_{p}={\bm{k}}\cdot\hat{e}_{p}. These are the spinons and the spinon dispersion on the triangular lattice is plotted in Fig. 9, and that on the square lattice in Fig. 10.

Notice that the spinons are gapped, and their minimum gaps are at two degenerate points in the Brillouin zone for both lattices. For the square lattice, the minima are at 𝒌=±(�/2,�/2){\bm{k}}=\pm(\pi/2,\pi/2) with an energy gap of (�¯2−4​J2​𝒬¯2)1/2\left(\bar{\lambda}^{2}-4J^{2}\bar{\mathcal{Q}}^{2}\right)^{1/2}. For the triangular lattice they are at 𝒌=±(4​�/3,0){\bm{k}}=\pm(4\pi/3,0) (and at wavevectors separated from these by reciprocal lattice vectors). So there are a total of 4 spinon excitations in both cases: 2 associated with the spin degeneracy of Sz=±1/2S_{z}=\pm 1/2, and 2 associated with the degeneracy in the Brillouin zone spectrum.

Next, we turn to spin-singlet excitations, i.e. understanding the nature of the spectrum of the 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} and �i\lambda_{i} fluctuations about the saddle point described above. At the outset, it appears that we can view such fluctuations as composites of 2-spinon excitations, as both 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} and �i\lambda_{i} couple to spinon pair operators, and so conclude that such excitations should not be viewed as the ‘elementary’ excitations of the quantum state found so far. Furthermore, the saddle-point has not broken any global symmetries of the Hamiltonian, and so it would appear that no such composite excitations has any reason to be low energy without fine-tuning.

However, it does turn out that there are separate elementary excitations in the singlet sector, and these arise from two distinct causes: (i) the gauge invariance in (28) leads to a gapless “photon” excitation; (ii) there are topologically non-trivial configurations of 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} which lead to excitations which appear as new saddle points. Excitations in the class (i) arise in the square lattice case, while those in class (ii) appear on the triangular lattice, and these will be considered separately in the following subsections.

3.2 Gauge excitations

The gauge transformations in (28) act on the phases of the 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, and so it is appropriate to just focus on the fluctuations of the phases of the 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} whose amplitudes are non-zero at the saddle-point.

3.2.1 Square lattice

We define

𝒬𝒊,𝒊+x^\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{x}} =\displaystyle= 𝒬¯​exp⁡(i​�𝒊​x)\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{Q}}\exp\left(i\Theta_{{\bm{i}}x}\right)

Then, taking the continuum limit of (37) with �𝒊​(�)=�𝒊​�​(r,�)\rho_{{\bm{i}}}(\tau)=\eta_{{\bm{i}}}\rho(r,\tau), we deduce from (38) that

As in traditional field-theoretic analyses, (39) imposes the requirement that the long-wavelength action of the a�a_{\mu} fluctuations must have the form

and this describes a gapless a�a_{\mu} photon excitation, with a suitable velocity of ‘light’. So, on the square lattice, the spectrum of spin-singlet states includes a linearly-dispersing photon mode. Such a state is a U(1) spin liquid. Actually, the gapless photon of this U(1) spin liquid is ultimately not stable because of monopole tunneling events; this involves a long and interesting story [5, 6, 26, 27] which we will discuss briefly in Section 3.5. For now, in the following subsection, we will consider the case of the triangular lattice, where, the U(1) photon is gapped by the Higgs mechanism to yield a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid.

3.2.2 Triangular lattice

This is a necessary condition for mapping the present state onto a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid (the reason for this nomenclature will become clearer in the following subsection).

The presentation so far of the gauge fluctuations described by a charge ±2\pm 2 Higgs field coupled to a U(1) gauge field would be appropriate for an anisotropic triangular lattice in which the couplings along the e^3\hat{e}_{3} direction are different from those along e^1\hat{e}_{1} and e^2\hat{e}_{2}. For an isotropic triangular lattice, all three directions must be treated equivalently, and then there is no simple way to take the continuum limit in the gauge sector: we have to work with the action in (49), but with the invariants specified as in (44). Such an action does not have a gapless photon anywhere in the Brillouin zone, and all gauge excitations remain gapped. There are other choices for the wavevector 𝒈{\bm{g}} in (45) at which the other pairs of values of cos⁡(kp/2)\cos(k_{p}/2) vanish; these are the points

which are related to the analysis above by the rotational symmetry of the triangular lattice.

3.3 Topological excitations on the triangular lattice

The analysis in Section 3.2 described small fluctuations in the phases of the 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} about their saddle-point values 𝒬¯\bar{\mathcal{Q}}. On the triangular lattice, we found that such fluctuations led only to gapped excitations, which at higher energies become part of the two-spinon continuum.

Now we consider excitations which involve large deviations from the spatially uniform saddle point values, and which turn out to be topologically protected. These excitations are closely connected to the vortices in charged superfluids. Consider a scalar field \Psi with charge qq coupled to the electromagnetic U(1) gauge field 𝑨{\bm{A}}. This has stable vortex-like saddle points with flux n​�0n\Phi_{0}, with �0=h​c/q\Phi_{0}=hc/q, for all integer nn. We have seen above that the on the triangular lattice, the Schwinger boson state has fluctuations described by a charge 2 Higgs field HH coupled to a U(1) gauge field a�a_{\mu}. In this case, we are normalizing the gauge field so that ˜​h​c⇒1\mathord{\mathchar 126h}c\Rightarrow 1, and so we can expect vortex solutions with a�a_{\mu} flux n⁡(2​�)/2n(2\pi)/2, for all integer nn. However, this is not quite correct. A crucial difference between the present theory and the electromagnetic gauge field is that the a�a_{\mu} gauge field is ‘compact’: this mean that a gauge field ax,ya_{x,y} is identical to ax,y+2​�a_{x,y}+2\pi, and tunneling events which change the total flux by 2​�2\pi are allowed (these are ‘monopoles’, which will be considered further in Section 3.5). This means that all vortex solutions with even nn are identical to each other, as are those with odd nn. The n=0n=0 case corresponds to no vortex at all, and so there is only a single non-trivial vortex with n=1n=1 and flux �\pi. This is the sought-after vison. Note that because fluxes �\pi and −�-\pi are identical, the vison saddle point preserves time-reversal symmetry. Similar excitations appear in a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory, and hence the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid nomenclature.

In this section, we will obtain the vison saddle point solution by working with a lattice effective action: this is essential to account for the influence of the monopoles. So we look for spatially non-uniform solutions of the saddle-point equations (31) and (32). In general, solving such equations is a demanding numerical task, and so we will be satisfied with a simplified analysis which is valid when the spin gap is large. In the large spin gap limit, we can integrate out the Schwinger bosons, and write the energy as a local functional of the 𝒬𝒊​𝒋{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}. This functional is strongly constrained by the gauge transformations in (28): for time-independent 𝒬𝒊​𝒋{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, this functional takes the form

E[{𝒬𝒊​𝒋}]=−∑𝒊<j(�|𝒬𝒊​𝒋|2+�2|𝒬𝒊​𝒋|4)−K∑even​loops𝒬𝒊​𝒋𝒬j​k∗…𝒬ℓ​i∗E[\{{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\}]=-\sum_{{\bm{i}}<j}\left(\alpha|{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}|^{4}\right)-K\sum_{{\rm even\,loops}}{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}{\mathcal{Q}}_{jk}^{\ast}\ldots{\mathcal{Q}}_{\ell i}^{\ast} (51)

Here �\alpha, �\beta, and KK are coupling constants determined by the parameters in the Hamiltonian of the antiferromagnet. We have shown them to be site-independent, because we have only displayed terms in which all links/loops are equivalent; they can depend upon links/loops for longer range couplings provided the full lattice symmetry is preserved.

We can now search for saddle points of the energy functional in (51). Far from the center of the vison, we have |𝒬𝒊​𝒋v|=𝒬¯|\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}|=\bar{\mathcal{Q}}, so that the energy differs from the ground state energy only by a finite amount. Closer to the center there are differences in the magnitudes. However, the key difference is in the signs of the link variables, as illustrated in Fig. 11: there is a ‘branch-cut’ emerging from the vison core along which sgn​(𝒬𝒊​𝒋v)=−sgn​(𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋)\mbox{sgn}(\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}})=-\mbox{sgn}(\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}). The results of a numerical minimization [28] of E⁡[{𝒬𝒊​𝒋}]E[\{{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\}] on the the triangular lattice are shown in Fig. 11.

The magnitudes of 𝒬𝒊​𝒋v\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} are suppressed close to the vison, and converge to 𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} as we move away from the vison (modulo the sign change associated with the branch cut), analogous to those in Abrikosov vortices. Despite the branch-cut breaking the 3-fold rotation symmetry, the gauge-invariant fluxes of 𝒬𝒊​𝒋v\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} preserve the rotation symmetry.

So we have found a stable real-vortex solution which preserves time-reversal, and has a finite excitation energy. We have also anticipated that this vortex will be identified with the vison particle of the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid: more evidence for this identification will appear in Sections 3.4.2 and 3.4.3.

3.4 Dynamics of excitations on the triangular lattice

For the case of the triangular lattice, Sections 3.1 and 3.3 have identified two types of elementary excitations: bosonic spinons with a 2-fold spin and a 2-fold lattice degeneracy, and a topological excitation which we have anticipated will become with vison particle of a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid. We will now describe the dynamics of the interactions between these excitations, and indeed verify that they reproduce the general structure associated with the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid.

A similar analysis can also be carried for the U(1) spin liquid on the square lattice. However, defer consideration of this case to Section 3.5.

3.4.2 Motion of visons

Let us now consider the motion of the vison elementary excitation, which we illustrated earlier in Fig. 13. The vison is located at the center of a triangle, and so can tunnel between neighboring triangular cells. We are interested here in any possible Berry phases the vison could pick up upon tunneling around a closed path.

In Section 3.3, we characterized the vison by the saddle-point configuration 𝒬𝒊​𝒋v\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} of the bond variables in the Hamiltonian (29). By diagonalizing this Hamiltonian [3, 28], we can show that the wavefunction of the vison can be written as

|⟩v=𝒫exp(∑𝒊<jf𝒊​𝒋v𝒥�​�b𝒊​�†bj​�†)|0⟩,\left|{}^{v}\right\rangle=\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\sum_{{\bm{i}}<j}f_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{v}\,\mathcal{J}_{\alpha\beta}b_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}b_{j\beta}^{\dagger}\right)|0\rangle, (79)

where |0⟩|0\rangle is the boson vaccum, 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a projection operator which selects only states which obey (19), and the boson pair wavefunction f𝒊​𝒋v=−fj​ivf^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=-f^{v}_{ji} is determined from (29) by a Bogoliubov transformation.

Let us now consider the motion of a single vison [28]. The gauge-invariant Berry phases are those associated with a periodic motion, and so let us consider the motion of a vison along a general closed loop 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We illustrated the simple case where 𝒞\mathcal{C} encloses a single site of the triangular lattice in Fig. 13.

The wavy lines indicate sgn​(𝒬𝒊​𝒋v)=−sgn​(𝒬¯𝒊​𝒋)\mbox{sgn}(\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}})=-\mbox{sgn}(\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}), as in Fig. 11. The last state is gauge-equivalent to the first state, after the gauge transformation b𝒊�→−b𝒊�b_{{\bm{i}}}^{\alpha}\rightarrow-b_{{\bm{i}}}^{\alpha} only for the site ii marked by the filled circle. As long as the vison wavefunction can be chosen to be purely real, it is clear that no Berry phase is accumulated from the time-evolution of the wavefunction as the vison tunnels around the path 𝒞\mathcal{C}. However, there can still be a non-zero Berry phase because a gauge-transformation is required to map the final state to the initial state. The analysis in Fig. 13 shows that the required gauge transformation is

b𝒊�→−b𝒊�,\displaystyle b_{{\bm{i}}}^{\alpha}\rightarrow-b_{{\bm{i}}}^{\alpha}, for ii inside 𝒞\mathcal{C}
b𝒊�→b𝒊�,\displaystyle b_{{\bm{i}}}^{\alpha}\rightarrow b_{{\bm{i}}}^{\alpha}, for i outside 𝒞.\displaystyle\mbox{for $i$ outside $\mathcal{C}$}. (80)

By Eq. (19), each site has nb=2​Sn_{b}=2S bosons, and so the total Berry phase accumulated by |⟩v|{}^{v}\rangle is

�​nb×(number of sites enclosed by 𝒞).\pi n_{b}\times\left(\mbox{number of sites enclosed by $\mathcal{C}$}\right). (81)

For the important case of S=1/2S=1/2, the vison experiences a flux of �\pi for every site of the triangular lattice. This phase factor of �\pi is related to an ‘anomaly’ associated with the global U(1) boson number symmetry, and translational symmetry [32, 33, 34, 35], and was first noted in Refs. [36, 37] as a feature of Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids with half-integer spin. In particular, this result implies the RVB state is an odd Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid.

A notable feature of (81) is that the quantized integer value of nb=2​Sn_{b}=2S is important. Memory of this quantization was lost in the mean field theory of Section 3.1, which was sensible also for non-integer values of nbn_{b}. So inclusion of the vison fluctuations restores the quantization of spin. A more complete theory for the vison fluctuations appears below in Section 3.4.4.

3.4.3 Semions and fermions

Proceeding the identification of the present Schwinger boson spin liquid with the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid, we need to establish that the spinons and visons are mutual semions. This is immediately apparent from a glance at Figs. 11 and 14.

The 𝒬𝒊​𝒋v\mathcal{Q}^{v}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} transport the spinons from site to site, and for spinon encircling a vison in a large circuit, the only difference between the cases with and without the vison is the branch cut. This branch cut yields an additional phase of �\pi in the vison amplitude, and provides the needed phase for mutual semion statistics [1, 2].

We can now identify the ee, �\epsilon, and mm anyons, in the abstract topological characterization of the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid obtained from the toric code [4]. The ee anyon is the the Schwinger boson itself, b�b_{\alpha}. This is mutual semion with respect to the vison, and so we identify the vison with the mm particle. Finally, the �\epsilon anyon is obtained by the fusion �=e×m\epsilon=e\times m, and so the �\epsilon anyon is a bound state of ee and mm. The �\epsilon anyon is a fermion as can be deduced by computing the Berry phase associated with exchanging one bound state of ee and mm with another bound state, as shown in Fig. 15.

(Note that this ‘long-distance’ Berry phase is multiplied by the ‘short-distance’ vison motion phases discussed in Section 3.4.2.) It is quite remarkable that a microscopic theory of bosonic spins 𝑺{\bm{S}}, expressed in terms of fractionalized bosons s�s_{\alpha}, yields an excitation which is a fermion: this is one indication of the presence of long-range entanglement and topological order.

An alternative formulation of the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid on the triangular lattice proceeds by expressing the spins 𝑺{\bm{S}} in terms of Schwinger fermions f�f_{\alpha}. For the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid, the f�f_{\alpha} spinons would become the �\epsilon particles, and the bosonic ee would be the bound state of the f�f_{\alpha} and the mm vison. So ultimately, independent of whether we choose to fractionalize the 𝑺{\bm{S}} spins in terms of bosonic or fermionic partons, we obtain the same characterization of the observable excitations in the resulting Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid. This identity also extends to the symmetry transformations of the anyons, as has been shown in some detail on the triangular [38], square [39, 40] and kagome [41] lattices.

3.4.4 Complete Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory of spinons and visons

We now combine the above results for the dynamics of spinons and visons to write down a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory for the triangular lattice quantum antiferromagnet which couples the z𝒊​�z_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} to a dynamic Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field Z𝒊​𝒋Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} on the links of a 3-dimensional hexagonal lattice (i.e. stacked triangular lattices) [42, 43]:

Similarly, for quantum antiferromagnets on other two-dimensional lattices, we would work with a three dimensional lattice obtained by stacking the two-dimensional lattice. The Z𝒊​𝒋Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} descend from the 𝒬𝒊​𝒋\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} by fixing their magnitudes and allowing their signs to be dynamical via

𝒬𝒊​𝒋⇒|𝒬𝒊​𝒋|​Z𝒊​𝒋.\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\Rightarrow\left|\mathcal{Q}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\right|Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}. (83)

From Eq. (28), the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge transformation in Eq. (76) acts on the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field via

Z𝒊​𝒋→�𝒊​Z𝒊​𝒋​�𝒋.Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\rightarrow\mu_{\bm{i}}Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\mu_{\bm{j}}\,. (84)

The novel term in Eq. (82), beyond those found in the lattice gauge theory literature, is the prefactor of the exponential in the curly brackets: this is the Berry phase term for half-integer spin SS. It is a direct consequence of the presence of a background Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge charge on each site, as implied by Eqs. (19) and (80) [43], and so accounts of the motion of visons in a background �\pi flux.

The partition function in Eq. (82) has been studied by quantum Monte Carlo, and yields the phase diagram in Fig. 16.

Apart from the ordered antiferromagnet and the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid in Fig. 12, here we obtain a valence bond solid (VBS) state as a consequence of the Berry phase term [36, 37]. This is gapped state which preserves spin rotation invariance, but breaks lattice translational symmetry.

The transition from the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid to the VBS can be studied by integrating out the z�z_{\alpha} spinons from Eq. (82). This yields a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory for the visons in terms of the Z𝒊​𝒋Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} alone. It is convenient to express this Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory in Hamiltonian form on the triangular lattice, which has exactly the form familiar in the lattice gauge theory literature:

HZ2=−K∑△∏𝒊​𝒋∈△Z𝒊​𝒋−g∑𝒊​𝒋X𝒊​𝒋,H_{\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}}=-K\sum_{\triangle}\,\,\prod_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\in\triangle}Z_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}-g\sum_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}X_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\,, (85)

where X𝒊​𝒋X_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} are Pauli XX operators on the links of the triangular lattice. However, the Berry phase term in Eq. (82) does make a crucial difference in selecting the gauge-invariant sector of the Hilbert space of HZ2H_{\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}}. There are infinite number of Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge charges which commute with HZ2H_{\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}}, one on each site of the triangular lattice:

G𝒊=∏ℓ∋𝒊Xℓ,G_{\bm{i}}=\prod_{\ell\ni{\bm{i}}}X_{\ell}\,, (86)

where now ℓ\ell labels the links of the triangular lattice. The Berry phase of Eq. (82) implies that we should chose the sector with [36, 37, 44]

G𝒊=(−1)2​S.G_{\bm{i}}=(-1)^{2S}\,. (87)

For (−1)2​S=−1(-1)^{2S}=-1, this term is crucial in ensuring that the confinement transition from the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid leads to a VBS, and there is no trivial ground state at large gg.

The transition from the ordered antiferromagnet to the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid is not influenced by the Berry phase term (because the visons remains gapped at this transition), and is described by the O(4) Wilson-Fisher critical theory [45, 46]. However, there is an important difference in the structure of the observable order parameter. Note that z�z_{\alpha} was obtained from the continuum limit of the spinon s�s_{\alpha}, and so it is fractionalized degree of freedom, carrying a unit Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} charge. Correlators of z�z_{\alpha} are therefore not observable, only those of gauge-invariant bilinear combinations. This is denoted by stating the universality class of the transition is actually O(4)∗. This critical theory has the same exponents as the O(4) theory, but some observables in a finite geometry are different [47]. As the critical fields of the theory are fractionalized spinons, this is an example of a ‘deconfined critical point’.

Near the multicritical region where the 3 phases meet in Fig. 16, there could be additional deconfined criticality [43] associated with a U(1) gauge theory of fermionic spinons [48, 49, 50, 51] which we do not explore here.

The continuum theory also makes it easy to determine the fate of the antiferromagnet when the spin energy gap vanishes. We expect that z�z_{\alpha} will bose condense, and this will break the spin rotation symmetry; a term quartic in z�z_{\alpha} will be needed to stabilize the condensate. But z�z_{\alpha} carries a U(1) gauge charge, and so is not directly observable. Following the definitions of the underlying spin operators, it is not difficult to show that the gauge-invariant composite

𝓝=z�∗​��​�​z�∼�𝒊​𝑺𝒊\bm{\mathcal{N}}=z_{\alpha}^{\ast}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}z_{\beta}\sim\eta_{\bm{i}}{\bm{S}}_{\bm{i}} (92)

is just the Néel order parameter of Fig. 2.

However, there is an important ingredient that our low energy theory has not yet considered. These are non-perturbative fluctuations of a�a_{\mu} which are Dirac monopoles in 2+1 dimensional spacetime, which carry non-trivial Berry phases [6]. We will not carry out a full analysis here, and only note that these monopole Berry phases are closely connected to the vison Berry phases in Section 3.4.2 [36, 37]. An important result is that the spin liquid noted above is ultimately not a spin liquid. It is unstable to proliferation of monopoles, and ultimately confines a valence bond solid. But monopoles do not have a significant effect on the Néel state.

3.5.1 Quantum criticality

On general symmetry grounds, we extend Eq. (91) to a theory for the vicinity of the quantum critical point at which the spinon gap vanishes [52]:

𝒮U⁡(1)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{U(1)} =\displaystyle= ∫d3​x​(ℒz+ℒmonopole)+𝒮B\displaystyle\int d^{3}x\,\left(\mathcal{L}_{z}+\mathcal{L}_{\rm monopole}\right)+\mathcal{S}_{B}
ℒz\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{z} =\displaystyle= |(∂�−ia�)z�|2+g|z�|2+u(|z�|2)2+K(��​�​�∂�a�)2\displaystyle|(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu})z_{\alpha}|^{2}+g|z_{\alpha}|^{2}+u\left(|z_{\alpha}|^{2}\right)^{2}+K(\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda})^{2}
ℒmonopole\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm monopole} =\displaystyle= −y⁡(ℳa+ℳa†)\displaystyle-y\left(\mathcal{M}_{a}+\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\dagger}\right)
𝒮B\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{B} =\displaystyle= i​2​S​∑𝒊�𝒊​∫d​�​a𝒊​�.\displaystyle i2S\sum_{\bm{i}}\eta_{\bm{i}}\int d\tau\,a_{{\bm{i}}\tau}\,. (93)

The theory ℒz\mathcal{L}_{z} is also known as the C​P1\mdmathbb{CP}^{1} model. We have included monopoles ℳa\mathcal{M}_{a} in the gauge field a�a_{\mu}, and also the Berry phase of the spinons in the ground state in 𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{B}. This Berry phase is closely connected to the vison Berry phase in Section 3.4.2 [36, 37]: note the similarity of 𝒮B\mathcal{S}_{B} to the Berry phase term in curly brackets of the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} gauge field in Eq. (82).

As we tune the coupling gg in Eq. (93), we can expect the 2 phases shown in Fig. 17:
(i) Néel phase, g<gcg<g_{c}: the spinon z�z_{\alpha} condenses in a Higgs phase with ⟨z�⟩≠0\langle z_{\alpha}\rangle\neq 0. The a�a_{\mu} gauge field is Higgsed, and spin rotation symmetry is broken by opposite polarization of the spins on the two sublattices.
(ii) Valence bond solid (VBS), g>gcg>g_{c}: the spinons are gapped. For half-integer spin SS, there is broken translational symmetry by the crystallization of valence bonds in the pattern shown in Fig. 17.

We now obtain a potential gapless spin liquid if there is a continuous quantum phase transition at g=gcg=g_{c}. For half-integer spin SS, the single monopole terms in Eq. (93) average to zero at long wavelengths from the Berry phases, and only quadrupoled monopole terms survive. So we can simplify the continuum theory for the vicinity of the quantum critical point to [26, 27]

ℒz=|(∂�−ia�)z�|2+g|z�|2+u(|z�|2)2+K(��​�​�∂�a�)2−y4(ℳa4+ℳa†4),\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\mathcal{L}_{z}=|(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu})z_{\alpha}|^{2}+g|z_{\alpha}|^{2}+u\left(|z_{\alpha}|^{2}\right)^{2}+K(\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda})^{2}-y_{4}\left(\mathcal{M}_{a}^{4}+\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\dagger 4}\right)\,, (94)

where y4y_{4} is the quadrupoled monopole fugacity. There is ample numerical evidence that y4y_{4} is irrelevant near a possible critical point, and so the question reduces to whether the theory ℒz\mathcal{L}_{z} at y4=0y_{4}=0 exhibits a critical point which realizes a conformal field theory in 2+1 dimensions. This is a question that has been studied extensively in numerics, and it is clear that a ‘deconfined critical’ description is suitable over a substantial length scale: with fractionalized spinons interacting with a U(1) gauge field in the absence of monopoles [53, 54, 23, 55, 24, 56].

4 Fermionic spinon theory of quantum spin liquids

We now present an alternative analysis of the square lattice antiferromagnet in Eq. (17), replacing the bosonic partons in Eq. (21) by fermionic partons. This will ultimately lead to the same phase diagram as in Fig. 17, but with a dual description of the phases and the criticality. This dual fermionic description turns out to be the most efficient way to describe the connection between the critical spin liquid and dd-wave superconductivity in the doped antiferromagnet, as we will see in Section 6.

The following Schwinger fermion representation applies only for S=1/2S=1/2

∑�f𝒊​�†​f𝒊​�=1,for all 𝒊.\sum_{\alpha}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}=1\quad,\quad\mbox{for all ${\bm{i}}$}. (96)

4.1 Low energy SU(2) gauge theory.

Going beyond mean field theory, while still remaining on the lattice, we extend the mean field Hamiltonian in Eq. (4) to be invariant under space-dependent SU(2) gauge symmetries. To achieve this, we need to introduce a SU(2) gauge field U𝒊​𝒋=U𝒋​𝒊†U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger} on each lattice link upon which the SU(2) gauge transformation acts as

U𝒊​𝒋→V𝒊​U𝒊​𝒋​V𝒋†.U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\rightarrow V_{\bm{i}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}V_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}\,. (110)

Then, by gauge invariance, we extend Eq. (4) to

ℋS​L​f\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{SLf} =\displaystyle= i​J2​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋​[Tr​(ℱ𝒊†​U𝒊​𝒋​ℱ𝒋)−Tr​(ℱ𝒋†​U𝒋​𝒊​ℱ𝒊)]\displaystyle\frac{iJ}{2}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left[\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)-\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)\right]
=\displaystyle= iJ∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋(U𝒊​𝒋†𝒊−𝒋U𝒋​𝒊†𝒋)𝒊;≡𝒊(f𝒊↑f𝒊↓†),\displaystyle iJ\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left({}_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}{}_{\bm{j}}-{}_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}{}_{\bm{i}}\right);\quad{}_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right),

The first form in terms of ℱ\mathcal{F} makes both the SU(2) gauge invariance and the SU(2) spin rotation invariance explicit, while in the second form in terms of \Psi only the gauge invariance is explicit.

If we had not used the pure imaginary hopping in Eq. (4), then the mean-field Hamiltonian would break (‘Higgs’) the SU(2) gauge symmetry to a smaller symmetry. A ‘staggered flux’ ansatz which breaks the SU(2) down to U(1) has commonly been used in the literature [61]. However, it is now known that this U(1) spin liquid allows single monopole perturbations [62, 63] (unlike the quadrupole monopole perturbations in Eq. (94)), and such single monopole terms are expected to drive a strong instability to confinement. So we don’t consider the staggered-flux U(1) spin liquid.

The continuum formulation of this theory can be obtained by following the same procedure as in Section 3.5, but we have to carefully account for the SU(2) gauge symmetry. First, neglecting gauge fluctuations of U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} for now, let us write Eq. (4) in momentum space, in terms of the fermions ℱs​(𝒌)\mathcal{F}_{s}({\bm{k}}), where s=A,Bs=A,B is a sublattice index. Now the sublattices refer to sites with 𝒊x{\bm{i}}_{x} even and odd, which are the two sites in the unit cell. We obtain

ℋS​L​f=−J∑𝒌Tr(ℱ†(𝒌)[�xsin(kx)+�zsin(ky)]ℱ†(𝒌)),\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{SLf}=-J\sum_{\bm{k}}\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}({\bm{k}})\left[\rho^{x}\sin(k_{x})+\rho^{z}\sin(k_{y})\right]\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}({\bm{k}})\right)\,, (114)

ℒ𝒳=i2Tr(𝒳¯[∂�−iA�ℓ�ℓ]�𝒳).\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}=\frac{i}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}{}^{\mu}\left[\partial_{\mu}-iA_{\mu}^{\ell}\sigma^{\ell}\right]\mathcal{X}\right)\,. (120)

The theory in Eq. (120) is the analog of the ℒz\mathcal{L}_{z} in Eq. (93) for bosonic spinons. The latter theory was a U(1) gauge theory with two relativistic complex scalars z�z_{\alpha}. In the present case, we have a SU(2) gauge theory with Nf=2N_{f}=2 massless Dirac fermions, associated with valley index vv. The global symmetry of z�z_{\alpha} was just spin rotations z→R​zz\rightarrow Rz. In contrast, here we have emergent global symmetry which combines spin and valley rotations. A first guess is a SU(4) symmetry generalizing Eq. (101)

𝒳→𝒳​L,\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}L\,, (121)

where LL acts on spin and valley space with L†​L=1L^{\dagger}L=1. However, imposition of the reality condition Eq. (98) shows that we also need

LT=�y​L†​�y,L^{T}=\sigma^{y}L^{\dagger}\sigma^{y}\,, (122)

and so the symmetry is only Sp(4)=SO(5)/Z2/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} [64, 11]. In terms of the Hermitian Lie algebra elements MM, with L=ei​ML=e^{iM}, the reality condition is

MT=−�y​M​�y.M^{T}=-\sigma^{y}M\sigma^{y}\,. (123)

Requiring that MM commute with the �, we can now write down the 10 elements of the Lie algebra of Sp(4)=SO(5)/Z2/\mdmathbb{Z}_{2}

M={�x,�y,�z,�z​�x,�z​�y,�z​�z,�x​�y,�x​�x​�x,�x​�x​�y,�x​�x​�z}.M=\{\sigma^{x},\sigma^{y},\sigma^{z},\mu^{z}\sigma^{x},\mu^{z}\sigma^{y},\mu^{z}\sigma^{z},\rho^{x}\mu^{y},\rho^{x}\mu^{x}\sigma^{x},\rho^{x}\mu^{x}\sigma^{y},\rho^{x}\mu^{x}\sigma^{z}\}\,. (124)

The remaining 5 SU(4) generators which commute with the � are (t=1​…​5t=1\ldots 5)

�t={�z,�x​�x,�x​�y​�x,�x​�y​�y,�x​�y​�z}.\Gamma^{t}=\{\mu^{z},\rho^{x}\mu^{x},\rho^{x}\mu^{y}\sigma^{x},\rho^{x}\mu^{y}\sigma^{y},\rho^{x}\mu^{y}\sigma^{z}\}\,. (125)

The �t\Gamma^{t} all anti-commute with each other, and transform as a SO(5) vector under the generators in Eq. (124). It is now straightforward to check by working back to the lattice operators from the information above that the vector i​Tr​(𝒳¯​�t​𝒳)i\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{t}\mathcal{X}\right) corresponds precisely to the 5 components of the orders parameters shown in Fig. 17: the first two components are the VBS order, and the last 3 components are the Néel order 𝓝\bm{\mathcal{N}} in Eq. (92) [64, 11].

Wang et al. [11] have argued that the likely fate of the SU(2) gauge theory upon confinement is a state which the SO(5) symmetry is spontaneously broken with ⟨i​Tr​(𝒳¯​�t​𝒳)⟩≠0\langle i\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{t}\mathcal{X}\right)\rangle\neq 0. The lattice model does not have exact SO(5) symmetry, and the choice between the Néel and VBS components of �t\Gamma^{t} is made by additional 4-fermi terms that can be added to Eq. (120). So the ultimate fate of the theory is essentially identical to the fate of the bosonic spinon theory in Section 3.5.1, as illustrated in Fig. 17. This is essentially the reason for the duality between the theories in Section 3.5.1 and 4.1, and Wang et al. have provided additional topological arguments.

4.2 SO(5) non-linear �\sigma-model

There is a third formulation of the theories in Section 3.5.1 and 4.1 which is useful for some purposes, as we illustrate in Fig. 20.

This is obtained most simply by coupling Eq. (120) to the SO(5) vector order parameter, and integrating out the fermions. Introducing the SO(5) fundamental unit length field ntn_{t}, nt​nt=1n_{t}n_{t}=1 to Eq. (120)

ℒ𝒳​n=i2Tr(𝒳¯[∂�−iA�ℓ�ℓ]�𝒳)−intTr(𝒳¯�t𝒳),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}n}=\frac{i}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}{}^{\mu}\left[\partial_{\mu}-iA_{\mu}^{\ell}\sigma^{\ell}\right]\mathcal{X}\right)-in_{t}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{t}\mathcal{X}\right)\,, (126)

we integrate out the Dirac fermions following the analysis of Ref. [65] and obtain

ℒn=12​g​(∂�nt)2+2​�​i​�​[nt]\mathcal{L}_{n}=\frac{1}{2g}\left(\partial_{\mu}n_{t}\right)^{2}+2\pi i\Gamma[n_{t}] (127)

The last term is the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) term at level 1: it is a Berry phase associated with spacetime textures of ntn_{t}, a higher dimensional analog of the Berry phase of a single spin which is proportional to area enclosed by a spherical path [66, 11]: an explicit expression of �⁡[nt]\Gamma[n_{t}] requires 4+1 dimensions with an emergent spatial direction. Upon reduction to a O(3) non-linear sigma model for the Néel order parameter 𝓝\bm{\mathcal{N}} in Eq. (92), the WZW term reduces [67] to the Berry phases of the monopoles noted near Eq. (94).

Also, note that while the SO(5) symmetry is explicit in the fermionic spinon theory in Eq. (120), it is not explicit in the bosonic spinon theory in Eq. (94), but expected to be emergent [68].

The form in Eq. (127) has been exploited in recent numerical work on the fuzzy sphere [56]. Their results, and those of a number of other numerical works [69, 53, 21, 22, 54, 23, 55, 24] show that the critical spin liquid defined by Eq. (94), Eq. (120), or (127) is stable over a substantial intermediate energy and length scales, before ultimately confining into a Néel or VBS state. This intermediate range stability is not a bug, but a feature ideal for our purpose in Section 7 of defining a FL* state at intermediate temperatures, which ultimately confines to variety of other states at low temperatures.

5 Holon metal from a quantum spin liquid with bosonic spinons

This section dopes the spin liquid state of Section 3.1 with holes of density pp. We already discussed the fate of the ordered antiferromagnet upon doping in Section 2, and here we will discuss the fate of the spin liquid.

For the Néel state in Section 2 we obtained a Fermi liquid metal with hole pockets of spin-1/2, charge ee quasiparticles. After accounting for the doubling of the unit cell, there are 2 independent pockets in Fig. 6, and so the fractional area of each pocket is p/4p/4.

In the present section, doping the spin liquid will yield a holon metal, which has Fermi pockets of spinless, charge ee quasiparticles, i.e. holons. There is no doubling of the unit cell here, and we will see that there are 4 independent pockets. So the area of each holon pocket is again p/4p/4. But such pockets are not directly observable in photoemission, as the electron operator is a composite of a holon and a spinon. However the holon pockets will contribute to magnetotransport observables restricted to motion within each square lattice plane.

We will argue in Section 7 that the holon metal does not provide a satisfactory description of the cuprate pseudogap. However, recent work [14, 15] has argued that the holon metal descending from a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid is indeed appropriate for the Hubbard model on the Lieb lattice.

A popular way to dope a spin liquid is to introduce a fermionic holon hh, so that the electron operator can be written as

c𝒊​�=h𝒊†​b𝒊​�.c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}=h_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}b_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,. (128)

However, this approach runs into complications associated with the sublattice assignment of opposite U(1) gauge charges in Eq. (88). We shall instead follow a simpler approach which is ultimately equivalent to Eq. (128), but is applicable more broadly. The central idea here is to transform the electron operator into a rotating reference frame in spin space [70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81, 15]

(c𝒊,↑c𝒊,↓)=Ri​(𝒊,+𝒊,−),R𝒊†​R𝒊=R𝒊​R𝒊†=𝟙.\left(\begin{array}[]{c}c_{{\bm{i}},\uparrow}\\ c_{{\bm{i}},\downarrow}\end{array}\right)=R_{i}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}{}_{{\bm{i}},+}\\ {}_{{\bm{i}},-}\end{array}\right),\quad\quad R_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}R_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}=R_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}R_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}=\mathds{1}. (129)

The fermions in the rotating reference frame are spinless ‘chargons’ s, with s=±s=\pm, carrying the electromagnetic charge. The SU(2) rotation matrix R𝒊R_{{\bm{i}}} is represented by two complex numbers

R𝒊=(z𝒊,↑−z𝒊,↓∗z𝒊,↓z𝒊,↑∗),|z𝒊,↑|2+|z𝒊,↓|2=1.R_{\bm{i}}=\begin{pmatrix}z_{{\bm{i}},\uparrow}&-z_{{\bm{i}},\downarrow}^{*}\\ z_{{\bm{i}},\downarrow}&z_{{\bm{i}},\uparrow}^{*}\end{pmatrix},\qquad|z_{{\bm{i}},\uparrow}|^{2}+|z_{{\bm{i}},\downarrow}|^{2}=1. (130)

Indeed, we identify z�z_{\alpha} with the spinons of the spin liquid described by the complex scalars of the C​P1\mdmathbb{CP}^{1} field theory in Eq. (93). Note that ∑p=±𝒊,p†𝒊,p=∑�=↑,↓c𝒊,�†c𝒊,�\sum_{p=\pm}{}_{{\bm{i}},p}^{\dagger}{}_{{\bm{i}},p}=\sum_{\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow}c_{{\bm{i}},\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{{\bm{i}},\alpha}, so the density of the chargons is the same as that of the electrons.

A key property of the decomposition in Eq. (129) is that it introduces a SU(2) gauge invariance [74].

R𝒊\displaystyle R_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}} →R𝒊​W𝒊†\displaystyle\rightarrow R_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,W_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}
(𝒊,+𝒊,−)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}{}_{{\bm{i}},+}\\ {}_{{\bm{i}},-}\end{array}\right) →W𝒊​(𝒊,+𝒊,−),\displaystyle\rightarrow W_{\bm{i}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}{}_{{\bm{i}},+}\\ {}_{{\bm{i}},-}\end{array}\right)\,,

where W𝒊W_{\bm{i}} is the SU(2) matrix generating the gauge transformation. This gauge invariance is distinct from the SU(2) gauge invariance of the fermionic spinons in Section 4, which is instead associated with a transformation in pseudospin space.

We now apply this tranformation to the paramagnon theory in Eq. (4). Then, we write the Yukawa coupling between the paramagnon 𝑷𝒊{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{i}}} and the electrons as

It is easy to deduce from Eq. (136) that 𝑯{\bm{H}} transforms as an adjoint under the SU(2) gauge transformation

We can now use the SU(2) gauge theory of \psi, RR, and 𝑯{\bm{H}} to describe the phases of the Hubbard model. The many possibilities are discussed at some length in Refs. [74, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81, 15]. We limit ourselves here to the simplest case of the state obtained by rotationally averaging the Néel state of Section 2. The doped spin liquid so obtained, the holon metal, corresponds to condensing the Higgs field as

⟨𝑯𝒊⟩=�𝒊​(0,0,H0)\left\langle{\bm{H}}_{\bm{i}}\right\rangle=\eta_{{\bm{i}}}\,(0,0,H_{0}) (143)

The effective theory for the chargons \psi can be obtained from Eq. (4) after (i) replacing the electrons c𝒊​�c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} by the chargon i,s, (ii) replacing the paramagnon 𝑷𝒊{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{i}}} by the Higgs condensate in Eq. (143), and (iii) minimally coupling the \psi to the U(1) gauge field a�a_{\mu}. 𝒮=∫0�d�[\displaystyle\mathcal{S}=\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau\Biggl[ ∑𝒊,s(∂�−�−ia�)𝒊,s†−𝒊,s∑𝒊,𝒋,s,s′t𝒊​𝒋ei​a𝒊​𝒋𝒋,s†𝒊,s\displaystyle\sum_{{\bm{i}},s}{}^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}},s}(\partial_{\tau}-\mu-ia_{\tau}){}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\bm{i}},s}-\sum_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}},s,s^{\prime}}t_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}e^{ia_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}}{}^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}},s}{}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\bm{j}},s}

where t𝒊​𝒋t_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} are the hoppings corresponding to the dispersion "𝒌\varepsilon_{\bm{k}} in Eq. (4). At leading order, this yields chargon pockets of spinless fermions which are the same as the pockets of electrons in the ordered Néel state presented in Section 2. At higher order, the gauge field will renormalize the dispersion so that the pockets lose the reflection symmetry about the magnetic Brillouin zone boundary present in the Néel state: the Brillouin zone of the holon metal is the same as that of underlying antiferromagnet without symmetry breaking.

The holon metal in Eq. (144) is associated with a U(1) spin liquid. If we replace Eq. (143) by a non-collinear configuration, then we obtain a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid, as is argued to be the case on the Lieb lattice [15].

6 dd-wave superconductor and charge orders at half-filling
from a quantum spin liquid with fermionic spinons

We now turn to the fermionic spinon theory of an insulating square lattice spin liquid in Section 4. We wish to consider a more general situation in which the gap to charged excitations can vanish [82]. In the cuprates, gapless charged excitations appear when we dope the antiferromagnet. But we can also consider the case where the charge gap vanishes while the electronic density remains the same as in an insulator i.e. at half-filling. This section will focus on the simpler situation at half-filling, and the full treatment of the doped case is deferred to Section 7. It turns out that the effective action for the charged degrees of freedom is quite similar to that in the doped case, and so this is a sensible way to proceed.

At half-filling, there can be an emergent particle-hole symmetry, which simplifies considerations of quantum criticality. We can decrease the charge gap by describing the insulator by an underlying Hubbard model with on-site repulsion UU, and reducing the value of UU, or by adding additional off-site interactions. Such models have been considered in numerical studies [83, 84, 85, 86, 87, 88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 93, 94]. We will now show that the SU(2) gauge theory of Eq. (4.1) has fates other than those in Fig. 17 once charged excitations are included, the most interesting of which is a dd-wave superconductor with gapless nodal quasiparticles.

In terms of adiabatic continuity, this dd-wave superconductor is the same as the BCS superconductor observed in the cuprates. However, the dd-wave superconductor obtained in this section has one significant quantitative difference from the observations: it has a Lorentz-invariant form of its dispersion, with the two velocities only the square lattice diagonals, vFv_{F} and v�v_{\Delta}, being equal to each other (see Fig. 36B). The cuprates instead have vF≫v�v_{F}\gg v_{\Delta}. We will resolve this problem in an interesting manner in Section 7.7 when we consider the transition from FL* to a dd-wave superconductor in the doped case.

The only matter field in Section 4 is the fermion ℱ\mathcal{F}, which has electrical charge 0, spin 1/21/2, and is a gauge SU(2) fundamental. As we are allowing for charged fluctuations, we need to define an electron operator, which has charge −e-e, spin 1/21/2, and is a gauge SU(2) singlet. This directly leads us to introducing a boson BB, first introduced in Ref. [9], which has charge +e+e, spin 0, and is a gauge SU(2) fundamental, so that a composite of ℱ\mathcal{F} and BB will have the same quantum numbers as the electron (see also Ref. [95] for work on the honeycomb lattice). We now show that this information is sufficient to deduce an effective action for BB, and to reach our main conclusions. We will give a more microscopic definition of the field BB in the doped case later near Eq. (184).

First, similar to Eq. (97), we introduce a matrix notation for the electron 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the boson BB:

𝒞𝒊≡(c𝒊↑−c𝒊↓c𝒊↓†c𝒊↑†),B𝒊≡(B1​𝒊B2​𝒊),ℬ𝒊≡(B1​𝒊−B2​𝒊∗B2​𝒊B1​𝒊∗),\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}c_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}&-c_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\\ c_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}&c_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right)\,,\quad B_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{c}B_{1{\bm{i}}}\\ B_{2{\bm{i}}}\end{array}\right)\,,\quad\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}B_{1{\bm{i}}}&-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\ast}\\ B_{2{\bm{i}}}&B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\ast}\end{array}\right)\,,

all of which obey the reality condition analagous to Eq. (98). Then we write the fact that the electron operator is a composite of the boson BB (the ‘chargon’) and the spinon ℱ\mathcal{F} by

𝒞𝒊∼ℬ𝒊†​ℱ𝒊.\mathcal{C}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\sim\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}\,\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,. (152)

In terms of the matrix components, we can write Eq. (152) as

c𝒊​�†∼B1​𝒊​f𝒊​�†+B2​𝒊​"�​�​f𝒊​�,c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}\sim B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}+B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,, (153)

where "�​�\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta} is the unit antisymmetric tensor for spin SU(2) in Eq. (24). Comparing to the transformation to a rotating reference frame in spin space in Eq. (129) in Section 5, we see that Eq. (152) corresponds to a transformation to a rotating reference frame in Nambu pseudospin space, with ℬ𝒊\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}} serving as the rotation matrix [78]. The parton decomposition in Eqs. (152,153) can also be obtained explicitly from a path integral analysis of the Hubbard model [95].

Now we can use Eq. (152) to determine the symmetry transformations of ℬ\mathcal{B} from those of ℱ\mathcal{F}, using the fact the 𝒞\mathcal{C} is gauge invariant and transforms trivially under all symmetries. A boson with the same quantum numbers as our BB was introduced in earlier work [9, 57, 10], but with an important difference. In the earlier work, the expectation value of B†​BB^{\dagger}B was set to be equal to the doping density. That is not the case here, as we also include second order time derivatives in BB (see Eq. (163)), and the doping density also includes the density of fermionic holes (see Section 7.6).

The generalization of the SU(2) gauge transformation in Eq. (100) is

We now obtain an energy functional for BB in a Landau-type expansion [96]. Such a functional must also involve the gauge field U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} of Section 4 to maintain gauge invariance. The fermion ff experiences a �\pi flux with pure imaginary hopping, while the electron cc has purely real hopping with zero flux (in the absence of an applied physical magnetic field).
