A schematic global phase diagram is shown in Fig. 21, as a function of the tuning parameter rr, which is the ‘mass’ of BB.

  • •

    When rr is large and positive, then we can ignore the BB sector, and revert to the spinon only theory of Section 4. The low energy theory is Eq. (120), and we expect a confining insulator with either Néel or VBS order as the ground state.

  • •

    When rr is negative, BB condenses, and this has the salutary effect of making the gauge field AA massive, as in the Higgs phenomenon. In this case, a mean-field treatment of interactions in the bosonic sector by minimizing ℰ2​[B,U]+ℰ4​[B,U]\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U] is qualitatively valid.

For negative rr, Fig. 21 shows the phases obtained by minimizing the energy functional with nearest-neighbor interactions only, V11=V22=0V_{11}=V_{22}=0. Three phases are found:

  1. A.

    This state has charge stripe order with period 2, centered on the sites.

  2. B.

    A dd-wave superconductor, with �𝒊,𝒊+𝒙^=−�𝒊,𝒊+𝒚^\Delta_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{\bm{x}}}=-\Delta_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{\bm{y}}}.

  3. C.

    A “dd-density wave” state which has a staggered pattern of spontaneous current.

Including further neighbor interactions can induce other phases, including period-4 charge order and pair density waves [96, 97, 98]), as shown in Fig. 22.

The present theory of multiple orders should be contrasted from more conventional Landau theory approaches [99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106]. In our case, we employ a fractionalized order parameter BB, whose gauge-invariant composites can represent multiple ordering patterns and broken symmetries. Upon integrating strong gauge fluctuations of UU, the fractionalized approach will yield an effective action which is essentially the same as in the Landau theory. But an important advantage of the fractionalized approach is that allows a local description of the fermionic spectrum in the pseudogap metal at non-zero temperatures [98]. Moreover, an interesting feature of the fractionalized approach is that the gauge-invariant orders are degenerate in the quadratic energy functional ℰ2\mathcal{E}_{2}, and the degeneracy is broken only at quartic order in ℰ4\mathcal{E}_{4}. The fact that the leading term is degenerate provides a rationale for nearly-degenerate multiple competing or ‘intertwined’ orders [96]; Landau theory approaches [99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 105, 106] do not have any term in which the degeneracy is exact without fine-tuning.

Our primary interest for now is the dd-wave supercondutor, phase B. Remarkably, the structure of the �\pi-flux spin liquid, and consequently the �\pi-flux on BB leads to dd-wave pairing, and not ss-wave pairing. Also, once BB is condensed, we can identify c∼fc\sim f via Eq. (152), and so the electron spectral function will inherit nodal Bogoliubov quasiparticles from the massless Dirac spinons [58, 60, 107, 10, 108, 61]. The main phenomenological difficulty is that the Bogoliubov quasiparticles will have isotropic dispersion, as in Eq. (108) and Fig. 19, in contrast to observations [18]; we will address this difficulty in Section 7. However, other features of the dd-wave state obtained from the energy functional in Eq. (161) do match observations, including vortices with flux h/(2​e)h/(2e) (despite the boson BB having charge ee), and competing charge order halos of vortex cores.

Going beyond a classical treatment of BB and UU, we can consider a quantum lattice model to study the interplay of the full array of competing order parameters and deconfined criticality at half-filling. This is obtained by extending the energy functionals in Eq. (161) and the lattice fermion theory in Eq. (4.1) to

ℒ=∑𝒊|D�B𝒊|2+ℰ2[B,U]+ℰ4[B,U]+∑𝒊D�†𝒊+𝒊ℋS​L​f+ℒY​M[U].\mathcal{L}=\sum_{\bm{i}}|D_{\tau}B_{\bm{i}}|^{2}+\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U]+\sum_{\bm{i}}{}_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}D_{\tau}{}_{\bm{i}}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{L}_{YM}[U]\,. (163)

Here D�D_{\tau} represents a covariant time derivative with the SU(2) gauge field UU, and ℒY​M\mathcal{L}_{YM} is the lattice Yang-Mills Lagrangian for UU. We have added only a relativistic time derivative term for B^\hat{B}, which is the allowed term at half-filling with particle-hole symmetry. A recent lattice gauge theory simulation [109] provides evidence that Eq. (163) displays a deconfined quantum critical point separating the insulating Néel state from a dd-wave superconductor with nodal Bogoliubov quasiparticles. Away from half-filling, we will also have to include the hole pockets to be discussed in Section 7, and that will likely lead to difficulties with the sign problem.

7 Fractionalized Fermi liquids (FL*)

Our motivation for studying quantum spin liquids has been to find a basis for a theory of the cuprate phase diagram. Christos et al. proposed [96] that the appropriate spin liquid was precisely that observed in various numerical studies of square lattice antiferromagnets: this is the spin liquid described by the C​P1\mdmathbb{CP}^{1} theory of Section 3.5.1, which is dual to the SU(2) gauge theory of fermionic spinons in Section 4. The previous sections have shown that the theories of directly doping such spin liquids run into difficulties:

  • •

    Doping the C​P1\mdmathbb{CP}^{1} spin liquid yields a holon metal state described in Section 5, which is a candidate for the pseudogap metal. However, as we discuss in Section 7.2.1, the holon metal is incompatible with recent angle-dependent magnetoresistance (ADMR) experiments [16, 17].

  • •

    The fermionic spin liquid can lead to a dd-wave superconductor, as described in Section 6. However, the velocities of the nodal quasiparticles are nearly isotropic, with vF∼v�v_{F}\sim v_{\Delta} [18].

We now show that replacing the holon metal with another doped spin liquid phase, the fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*), resolves both (and other) difficulties above. It agrees with the ADMR measurements in the pseudogap, and a confinement transition from FL* yields a dd-wave superconductor with anisotropic nodal velocities.

We begin by presenting the basic definition of the FL* state. Consider any system of S=1/2S=1/2 fermions of density �\rho, with spin rotation invariance preserved. In the Fermi liquid (FL) state, Luttinger’s argument [110] states that the fractional volume of the Brillouin zone enclosed by the Fermi surface should be �/2\rho/2, modulo integers to account for filled bands. Oshikawa [111] placed Luttinger’s argument on a non-perturbative basis by presenting a flux-piercing argument which has a modern interpretation as an ‘anomaly’ associated with translations and charge conversation; see Ref. [112] for a review. This is summarized in Fig. 23.

The idea of a ‘fractionalized Fermi liquid’ (FL*) was introduced in Refs. [19, 20], as a metallic state in which the Fermi surface did not obey the Luttinger constraint. In the simplest case, the fractional volume enclosed by the Fermi surface in FL* is (�−1)/2(\rho-1)/2. As stated in Ref. [19]:

“The primary purpose of this paper is to show that there exist nonmagnetic, metallic states (FL*) in dimensions d≥2d\geq 2 with a Fermi surface of ordinary S=1/2S=1/2, charge ee, sharp quasiparticles, enclosing a volume

𝒱FL∗=𝒦d​[(�a−1)​(mod2)],\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{FL}^{*}}=\mathcal{K}_{d}\left[(\rho_{a}-1)(\mathrm{mod2})\right],

over a finite range of parameters.”

(Here, �a\rho_{a} is the total electron density, 𝒦d=(2​�)d/(2​v0)\mathcal{K}_{d}=(2\pi)^{d}/(2v_{0}) is a phase space factor, v0v_{0} is the volume of the unit cell, and the (mod 2) accounts for filled bands which we ignore here.) The central point [19, 20, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 32, 33, 112, 34, 35] was that it was possible to satisfy Oshikawa’s anomaly-argument by combining the anomaly of a Fermi surface, which contributes an amount equivalent to a density �−1\rho-1, with that of a fractionalized spin liquid, which contributes a quantized amount equivalent to a density 1; the results in Eqs. (81), (87), (127) are realizations of such a quantized spin liquid anomaly [11, 118]. It is trivially possible to shift �\rho by an even integer by adding and removing filled bands, and the novelty is the shift in FL* by an odd integer; note that the shift in density cannot be arbitrary and is quantized by the structure of the spin liquid. The properties of the FL* state are summarized in Fig. 24.

We emphasize that the spin liquid is not required to have a spinon Fermi surface to compensate for the missing Luttinger volume in the FL* state. It is only required that its Oshikawa anomaly be an odd integer.

7.1 Generalized Luttinger constraints

The conventional proof of the Luttinger theorem for a Fermi liquid [110] rests on an all orders expansion from a free fermion state, and shows that the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface depends only the density of fermions, and is independent of the strength of interactions. The proof involves certain assumptions on the structure of the perturbative expansion, which will be specified below.

In this subsection, we will present Luttinger’s analysis in a more general context [114, 115]. Rather than starting from a free fermion state, we will start with a simple saddle-point of a parton theory of a fractionalized metallic state. The perturbative expansion from this saddle point will necessarily involve emergent gauge fields, but this does not preclude application of Luttinger’s methods as long the perturbative expansion does not lead to an instability of the saddle point (which we assume). This generalized analysis also leads to constraints on the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface, but the constraints are distinct from those of Luttinger.

As an example of a parton theory, consider the parton decomposition in Eq. (128) of an electron into a spinful, neutral boson b�b_{\alpha}, and a spinless fermionic holon, hh, of charge ee. Associated with this parton decomposition is an emergent U(1) gauge invariance, and a constraint

b𝒊​�†​b𝒊​�+h𝒊†​h𝒊=1,b_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}b_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}+h_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}h_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}=1\,, (164)

which fixes a unit background gauge charge on each site. Note that the value of the r.h.s. of Eq. (164) is a rigid property of the spin liquid which does not change upon doping. It is this background gauge charge which is responsible for or the quantized Berry phase in Eq. (81) of �\pi for a vison encircling each site in a Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [36, 37], and the quantized monopole Berry phase [6] for the C​P1\mdmathbb{CP}^{1} spin liquid of Section 3.5. We will see an explicit example of the constraint Eq. (164) being obeyed for the doped case in the quantum dimer model [119] discussed near Fig. 27.

Distinct from the U(1) gauge invariance, we also have a global U(1) symmetry associated with the conservation of electron density �\rho. In the parton formulation, an electron density 1 has been absorbed by the background gauge charge of the spin liquid, and the global density constraint is on the density of holons

⟨h𝒊†​h𝒊⟩=�−1.\left\langle h_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}h_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right\rangle=\rho-1\,. (165)

The −1-1 on the r.h.s. of Eq. (165) is therefore directly connected to the 1 in r.h.s. of Eq. (164).

As a second example of a parton theory, consider the SU(2) spin liquid of Section 4, which has neutral fermionic spinons f�f_{\alpha}, and a doublet (B1,B2)(B_{1},B_{2}) of spinless, charge ee bosons upon doping in Section 6. In the parton formulation of Ref. [10], the analog of the gauge charge constraint in Eq. (164) is

f𝒊​�†​f𝒊​�+B1​𝒊†​B1​𝒊−B2​𝒊†​B2​𝒊=1,f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}+B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}=1\,, (166)

and there is a similar constraint in the rotor formulation of Ref. [95]. The r.h.s. of Eq. (166) is quantized by the SU(2) gauge symmetry. Now the global electron number symmetry leads to a constraint on the density of bosons

⟨B1​𝒊†​B1​𝒊⟩+⟨B2​𝒊†​B2​𝒊⟩=�−1,\left\langle B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right\rangle+\left\langle B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right\rangle=\rho-1\,, (167)

in contrast to the density of fermions in Eq. (165).

Next, we follow the analysis of Ref. [114] to determine the low energy consequences of the microscopic constraints associated with electron number conservation given in Eqs. (165) and (167). Any renormalized theory must have a global U(1) electron number symmetry with a net charge matching that in Eqs. (165,167). We assume that the renormalized theory is well described by a set of fields FsF_{s} carrying charges qsq_{s} under this global U(1) symmetry, so that the theory is invariant under

Fs→Fs​ei​qs​�.F_{s}\rightarrow F_{s}e^{iq_{s}\theta}\,. (168)

The FsF_{s} fields can be fermions or bosons, and will generally always include the parton fields of the microscopic theory. However, there can also be additional fields, associated with ‘molecular’ bound states of the partons. These bound states are associated with a pole in a parton-parton scattering TT-matrix: such a pole can be replaced by the propagator of a canonical fermion or boson field representing the ‘molecule’, along with a coupling allowing decay of the ‘molecule’ into the ‘atomic’ partons: see Fig. 25.

With such a representation, it is possible to systematically treat the situation with a finite densities of partons and their bound states [114, 120, 121, 122]. This process is similar to the ‘two channel’ approach to the Feshbach resonance [123, 124, 125], and effective field theories in nuclear physics [126]. In particular, we include a ‘molecular’ fermionic field which has the same quantum numbers as the electron, c~�\widetilde{c}_{\alpha}, as a renormalized quasiparticle obtained as a bound state of a spinon and a holon [127, 128, 116]. The complete set of low energy fields is difficult to specify in advance for a particular Hamiltonian, but a posteriori the requirement is that the Luttinger-type analysis is well behaved, as we will clarify below. We will present an explicit derivation of such a renormalized theory in the discussion on the ancilla model in Section 7.3.

In a perturbative Feynman graph analysis [129], the renormalized theory is characterized by corresponding renormalized Green’s functions Gs​(𝒑,i​!)G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega) and self energies �s​(𝒑,i​!)\Sigma_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega) (assumed diagonal in the field index for convenience) which are related by a Luttinger-Ward functional �L​W​[Gs]\Phi_{LW}[G_{s}]

�s​(𝒑,i​!)=&s​�​�L​W�​Gs​(𝒑,i​!),\Sigma_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)=\varsigma_{s}\frac{\delta\Phi_{LW}}{\delta G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)}\,, (169)

where &s=−1​(+1)\varsigma_{s}=-1(+1) for fermions (bosons). An important property of the Luttinger-Ward functional, following from the global U(1) symmetry in Eq. (168), is its invariance under frequency shifts

�⁡[Gs​(𝒑,i​!+i​qs​!0)]=�⁡[Gs​(𝒑,i​!)],\Phi\left[G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega+iq_{s}\omega_{0})\right]=\Phi\left[G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)\right]\,, (170)

for any fixed !0\omega_{0}. Here, we are regarding �\Phi as functional of two sets of distinct functions fs​1,s​2​(!)f_{s1,s2}(\omega), with fs​1​(!)≡Gs​(𝒑,i​!+i​!0)f_{s1}(\omega)\equiv G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega+i\omega_{0}) and fs​2​(!)=Gs​(𝒑,i​!)f_{s2}(\omega)=G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega), and �\Phi evaluates to the same value for these two functions.

In terms of the renormalized theory, the microscopic constraints in Eqs. (165) and (167) can be evaluated by computing the conserved global U(1) density:

�−1=−1V∑𝒑∑s&sqsds∫−∞∞d​!2​�Gs(𝒑,i!)ei​!​0+,\rho-1=-\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{s}\varsigma_{s}q_{s}d_{s}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)e^{i\omega 0^{+}}\,, (171)

where dsd_{s} is the spin degeneracy of particle ss. Now we can proceed along exactly the lines described by Luttinger [112]. We insert into Eq. (171) the following identity following directly from Dyson’s equation

Gs​(𝒑,i​!)=i​∂∂!​ln⁡[Gs​(𝒑,i​!)]−i​Gs​(𝒑,i​!)​∂∂!​�s​(𝒑,i​!).G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)=i\frac{\partial}{\partial\omega}\ln\left[G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)\right]-iG_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)\frac{\partial}{\partial\omega}\Sigma_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)\,. (172)

Then we can write

�−1=ℐ1​p+ℐ1​z+ℐ2\rho-1=\mathcal{I}_{1p}+\mathcal{I}_{1z}+\mathcal{I}_{2} (173)

where

ℐ1​p\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{1p} =\displaystyle= −iV∑𝒑∑s&sqsds∫−∞∞d​!2​�∂∂!ln[Gs(𝒑,i!)]ei​!​0+|only from poles of Gs\displaystyle-\left.\frac{i}{V}\sum_{\bm{p}}\sum_{s}\varsigma_{s}q_{s}d_{s}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\frac{\partial}{\partial\omega}\ln\left[G_{s}({\bm{p}},i\omega)\right]e^{i\omega 0^{+}}\right|_{\mbox{only from poles of $G_{s}$}}

(174)

The ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} term contains the conventional contribution of the Fermi surface where Gs−1​(𝒑,!=0)=0G_{s}^{-1}({\bm{p}},\omega=0)=0, while the ℐ1​z\mathcal{I}_{1z} is often called the contribution of the “Luttinger surface” where Gs​(𝒑,!=0)=0G_{s}({\bm{p}},\omega=0)=0.

Important ingredients in the conventional Luttinger arguments are that ℐ1​z=0\mathcal{I}_{1z}=0 and ℐ2=0\mathcal{I}_{2}=0. It is assumed that the perturbation theory is stable, there are no poles in the self energy �s\Sigma_{s}, and consequently no zeros in GsG_{s}, and so ℐ1​z\mathcal{I}_{1z} vanishes. The vanishing of ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} follows after taking the !0\omega_{0} derivative of Eq. (170), and integrating by parts in frequency. Then the conventional Luttinger area of �/2\rho/2 follows by evaluating ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} from the electron quasiparticle pole on the Fermi surface, with the l.h.s. in Eq. (173) equal to �\rho in this case.

For the parton theories being analyzed here, we obtain the FL* state by also assuming ℐ1​z=ℐ2=0\mathcal{I}_{1z}=\mathcal{I}_{2}=0 because of the stability of the parton perturbation theory. For ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p}, we assume that the only pole contribution is from the emergent electron-like holon-spinon bound state c~�\widetilde{c}_{\alpha}, and there is no contribution to ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} from any of the spinons and holons. Then we immediately obtain

OPEN�−1=2×(Area of c~� Fermi surfaces)\rho-1=2\times\mbox{(Area of $\widetilde{c}_{\alpha}$ Fermi surfaces}) (175)

i.e. the total area of the Fermi surfaces per spin is (�−1)/2(\rho-1)/2 (in units where the area of the Brillouin zone is 1), illustrated in Fig. 24.

There can also be contributions to ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} from the fermionic holons hh, and we obtain the holon metal state of Section 5 if this is the only non-zero contribution to ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} (and we have ℐ1​z=ℐ2=0\mathcal{I}_{1z}=\mathcal{I}_{2}=0). If there are contributions to ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} from both c~�\widetilde{c}_{\alpha} and hh, then we obtain a hybrid state called the ‘holon-hole metal’ [128].

We note that bosonic quasiparticles, such as B1,2B_{1,2} in Eqs. (166,167) cannot have zero frequency poles which contribute to ℐ1​p\mathcal{I}_{1p} [114]. Nevertheless Eq. (167) can be satisfied in a FL* state even though the l.h.s. has only boson number expectation values on the microscopic lattice scale—the contribution appears in the low energy theory from the appearance of spinon-holon bound states of B1,2B_{1,2} and f�f_{\alpha}.

There are numerous non-perturbative analyses in the literature in which ℐ1​z\mathcal{I}_{1z} and/or ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} are non-zero [130, 131, 132, 133, 134, 135, 136, 137, 138, 139, 140, 141, 142, 143, 144, 145, 146].

The non-vanishing of ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} requires breakdown of integration by parts over frequency, and this is possible if the local density of states is divergent at zero frequency. This happens for zero-dimensional models like the SYK model [144, 145, 146].

The non-vanishing of ℐ1​z\mathcal{I}_{1z} is associated with a pole in the self-energy, which indicates the appearance of a new particle in some intermediate channel.

This improved theory (which should also have ℐ2=0\mathcal{I}_{2}=0) will then provide a better handle on the true excitation spectrum of the state under consideration: this is the procedure we follow in Section 7.3.

7.2 FL* in single band models

We describe here explicit construction of the FL* phase in a single band model, such as the square lattice Hubbard model (possibly with additional short-range interactions) of interest for the cuprates. At the level of cartoon pictures, we illustrate the structure of the FL* and other states in Fig. 26 [119]. This figure describes three distinct metallic phases in a Hubbard time model with electron density 1−p1-p. Recall that in the absence of a broken symmetry, the Luttinger constraint on hole Fermi surfaces is that they have a fractional area per spin of (1+p)/2(1+p)/2, relative to the area of the full square lattice Brillouin zone.

  • •

    AF Metal. This is a state with antiferromagnetic long-range order, which we described in Section 2. We can understand the Fermi surface by considering free electrons moving in a background with the same symmetry i.e. in a background spin-dependent potential which has a modulation at the wavevector (�,�)(\pi,\pi). This leads to the magnetic Brillouin zone boundary shown by the dashed line, and 4 hole pocket Fermi surfaces. Only two of these pockets are independent within the magnetic Brillouin zone. After accounting for a factor of 2 from spin, we conclude that the fractional area of each pocket is p/4p/4. This Fermi surface area obeys the Luttinger constraint. Thermal fluctuations do not move Fermi surfaces, only broaden them, and so we expect that a fluctuating spin density wave state will also have pockets of area p/4p/4 [147, 148, 149, 150].

  • •

    Holon metal. This is a state with no broken symmetry, in which the electrons have paired up in singlet bonds which resonate with each other. The dopants are realized by spinless mobile vacancies of charge +e+e, known as holons. The density of holons is pp, and if the holons are fermions, they will form Fermi surfaces corresponding to spinless free fermions of density pp. If there are four distinct Fermi surfaces in the Brillouin zone (as is the case in many computations), then the fractional area of each pocket will be p/4p/4. Although this area is the same as that for the AF metal, the reason is very different. Now there is no broken symmetry, and the fermionic quasiparticles are spinless holons. This Fermi surface area does not obey the usual Luttinger constraint, and this is permitted because of the presence of the spin liquid, as discussed in Section 7.1. A systematic, gauge theoretic treatment of the holon metal state was presented in Section 5 [151, 75, 76, 77, 152, 153, 154, 79, 155, 80, 81], and it is relevant to ultracold studies of the Hubbard model on the Lieb lattice [14, 15]. The discussion below Eq. (144) explains the equality of pocket areas between the AF metal and the holon metal.

  • •

    FL*. Finally, we turn to the metallic state of interest. The holon metal state also has spinon excitations, which can be created out of the ground state. Now imagine a situation in which each holons gains energy by binding with a spinon, as in Fig. 25, so that the system can pay the price for creating the spinons. In a tt-JJ model with electron hopping tt, and exchange energy JJ, the cost for creating a spinon is order JJ, and the energy gain from the formation of the holon-spinon bound state is of order tt, and so this bound state formation is very likely in the natural situation with t≫Jt\gg J. Then the ground state will change into one in which the mobile charge carriers are holon-spinon bound states [156, 127, 128, 116, 157, 158, 159, 160, 161, 119, 162, 163, 164, 165, 166, 167]. These bound states, the c~�\widetilde{c}_{\alpha} of Fig. 25, are always fermions with charge +e+e, spin S=1/2S=1/2, just like a hole. Treating these holes as free fermions, we conclude that the total area of the Fermi surface should be p/2p/2. If there are 4 distinct pockets (as there in the computation below), then each pocket will have the distinctive area of p/8p/8. This Fermi surface area also does not obey the usual Luttinger constraint, but does obey the generalized Luttinger constraint discussed in Seçtion 7.1.

An important feature of the comparison above is the remarkable distinction between “thermally disordered” and “quantum disordered” antiferromagnets. The thermally disordered AF Metal has pockets of area p/4p/4, while the quantum-disordered FL* state has pockets of area p/8p/8. Computations which describe the pseudogap by computing hole motion in an ordered antiferromagnet [168, 169, 163], and then rotationally averaging to account for thermal disorder, miss important state-counting constraints of a quantum spin liquid.

We highlight key features of the single-band FL* state [119] in Fig. 26. We will see that these features will also play a key role in the Ancilla Layer Model of Section 7.3, as we illustrate later in Fig. 32.

The FL* picture in Fig. 26 was used to motivate an effective quantum dimer model for the FL* phase [119]. The Hilbert space is defined by the set of dimer packings on the square lattice with 2 species of dimers: blue dimers representing the spin-singlet valence bonds, and green dimers representing the charge +e+e, spin S=1/2S=1/2 bound states, with the blue dimers being bosons, while the green dimers are fermions. Note that every configuration of this dimer model obeys the unit gauge charge constraint of Eq. (164). An effective dimer Hamiltonian acts by rearranging dimer configurations on the Hilbert space. Exact diagonalization results on the dispersion spectrum of a single green dimer are shown in Fig. 27.

This dispersion has minima near (±�/2,±�/2)(\pm\pi/2,\pm\pi/2), and filling the low-lying states with a density pp of green dimers would yield the area p/8p/8 pockets of FL* sketched in Fig. 26.

7.2.1 ADMR

Recent ADMR observations [16, 17] in the pseudogap metal are well modeled by hole pockets containing quasiparticles which can tunnel coherently between layers. This is not possible for holon metals, as the holons carry charges of distinct emergent gauge fields within each layer. In the AF metal, coherent tunneling requires significant interlayer spin correlations, which are not observed [170, 171], but could perhaps be induced by the applied magnetic field. The FL* quasiparticles are gauge neutral and can indeed tunnel coherently between layers. So even at the outset, before any quantitative comparisons, these observations strongly favor a FL* description of the pseudogap phase of the cuprates [172].

Moreover, the observations [17] also provide a quantitative correspondence with the FL* theory. Their observation of the Yamaji effect in the cuprate HgBa2CuO4+� show pockets of a fractional area of ‘approximately 1.3%1.3\%’ at a doping p=0.1p=0.1, close to the value p/8=1.25%p/8=1.25\% predicted for FL* [19, 20, 127, 116, 173, 172, 174].

7.3 Layer construction with ancilla qubits

While much insight can be gained from the methods above, they fall short of providing a mean-field theory for the FL* phase, which could be used to study quantum phase transitions out of it. A suitable mean field theory can also lead to a trial wavefunction for the FL* state, which can be used for variational numerical computations and compared to cold atom observations [175, 176, 177, 178], as discussed in Section 7.5. To these ends, we now describe the Ancilla Layer Model (ALM) [179, 180], which is designed to automatically ensure consistency with anomaly-type arguments, which are equivalent to the generalized Luttinger constraints discussed in Section 7.1.

We wish to have a mean-field theory which changes a large hole-like Fermi surface of area (1+p)/2(1+p)/2 to small hole-like Fermi surfaces of total area p/2p/2. The simplest way to achieve this in mean-field theory is to hybridize the large Fermi surface with another band at half-filling (as in the Kondo lattice, and was done by Yang-Rice-Zhang (YRZ) [133, 174])—this leads to a Fermi surface of the needed area (1+p+1)/2(1+p+1)/2 (mod 1) =p/2=p/2. But we are not allowed to add a single band at half-filling because it is not ‘trivial’ i.e. it is not anomaly-free, and its excitations cannot be integrated out because the extra band can only acquire a gap with a broken symmetry. On the other hand, we are allowed to add two bands at half filling each (or any even number of bands), because they can form a trivial insulator with a gap. After the first added band hybridizes with the physical electrons to yield the small Fermi surfaces, the second added band is left decoupled, and it can form the spin liquid needed to satisfy the Oshikawa anomaly-argument and the constraints in Section 7.1. This is the essence of the ALM.

We begin with a constructive derivation of the ALM starting from the familiar Hubbard model in Eq. (1), and returning to the paramagnon representation in Eq. (4). After some renormalization of the high energy states we give the paramagnon 𝑷{\bm{P}} some independent dynamics with a non-zero mass m𝑷m_{{\bm{P}}}, and obtain its effective Lagrangian

ℒ⁡[𝑷]=∑𝒊[m𝑷2​(∂�𝑷𝒊)2+3​U8​𝑷𝒊2],\mathcal{L}[{\bm{P}}]=\sum_{\bm{i}}\left[\frac{m_{{\bm{P}}}}{2}\left(\partial_{\tau}{\bm{P}}_{\bm{i}}\right)^{2}+\frac{3U}{8}{\bm{P}}_{\bm{i}}^{2}\right]\,, (176)

where the 𝑷2{\bm{P}}^{2} term is as in Eq. (4). This is a paramagnon theory with 3 local harmonic oscillators of frequency (3​U/(4​m𝑷))1/2(3U/(4m_{{\bm{P}}}))^{1/2} on each site, which are coupled to the electrons with a Yukawa coupling of strength UU in Eq. (4) . Now we take steps different from conventional paramagnon approaches. The ground state of the paramagnon theory is obtained when all three oscillators are in the n=0n=0 state: |0,0,0⟩\left|0,0,0\right\rangle. There is a triplet of first excited states:

|1,0,0⟩∼𝑷𝒊​x|0,0,0⟩;|0,1,0⟩∼𝑷𝒊​y|0,0,0⟩;|0,0,1⟩∼𝑷𝒊​z|0,0,0⟩.\left|1,0,0\right\rangle\sim{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{i}}x}\left|0,0,0\right\rangle;\left|0,1,0\right\rangle\sim{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{i}}y}\left|0,0,0\right\rangle;\left|0,0,1\right\rangle\sim{\bm{P}}_{{\bm{i}}z}\left|0,0,0\right\rangle.

We can map this low energy spectrum to that of a pair of S=1/2S=1/2 ancilla spins with a mutual interaction J⟂​𝑺1​𝒊⋅𝑺2​𝒊J_{\perp}{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}. By comparing the above matrix elements to those that couple the singlet and triplet spin states states, we obtain the operator identification

𝑷𝒊∼𝑺1​𝒊−𝑺2​𝒊.{\bm{P}}_{\bm{i}}\sim{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}-{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}\,. (177)

Inserting Eq. (177) into Eq. (4), we obtain the Hamiltonian of the ALM, ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM}. This has a Kondo lattice Hamiltonian ℋKL\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL} with couples the electrons c�c_{\alpha} to the 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} spins by an antiferromagnetic Kondo coupling JK∼UJ_{K}\sim U, and a second layer of 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins which have a rung coupling J⟂=(3​U/(4​m𝑷))1/2J_{\perp}=(3U/(4m_{{\bm{P}}}))^{1/2} to the 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} spins:

ℋALM\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM} =ℋKL+J⟂​∑𝒊𝑺1​𝒊⋅𝑺2​𝒊+∑𝒊<𝒋J𝒊​𝒋​𝑺2​𝒊⋅𝑺2​𝒋\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL}+J_{\perp}\sum_{{\bm{i}}}{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}+\sum_{{\bm{i}}<{\bm{j}}}J_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\,{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{j}}}
ℋKL\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL} =∑𝒊<𝒋J1,𝒊​𝒋​𝑺1​𝒊⋅𝑺1​𝒋−∑𝒊,𝒋t𝒊​𝒋​c𝒊​�†​c𝒋​�+∑𝒊JK2​𝑺1​i⋅c𝒊​�†​��​�​c𝒊​�.\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{i}}<{\bm{j}}}J_{1,{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\,{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{j}}}-\sum_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}}}t_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}c_{{\bm{j}}\alpha}+\sum_{{\bm{i}}}\frac{J_{K}}{2}{\bm{S}}_{1i}\cdot c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}c_{{\bm{i}}\beta}\,. (178)

This Hamiltonian is illustrated in the bottom half of Fig. 28.

So we see that the ancilla spins are simply the fractionalization of the familiar S=1S=1 paramagnon into a pair of S=1/2S=1/2 spins [182]. The above derivation of the mapping to the ALM yields an additional ferromagnetic Kondo interaction between the electrons c𝒊​�c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} and spins 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}. Ferromagnetic Kondo couplings are expected to be irrelevant, and we will note this coupling again in Eq. (184). Note that it is Eq. (177) which breaks the symmetry between 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} and 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2}, and we choose the spins in the middle layer to be the ones which have the antiferromagnetic Kondo coupling with the electrons. We have also explicitly included a direct exchange interaction between the 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} spins, as it will be important for our purposes below. Note also that there is no Hubbard interaction UU in ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM}, and it has been replaced by the Kondo interaction JKJ_{K} in ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM}.

We summarize the phase diagram of ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM} in Fig. 29.

At small JKJ_{K}, the ancilla spins decouple into rung singlets, and we are back to a c�c_{\alpha} state adiabatically connected to free electrons, which is the conventional Fermi liquid with a large hole pocket of area (1+p)/2(1+p)/2.

At large JKJ_{K}, we assume that the c�c_{\alpha} electrons and 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} spins realize the commonly observed heavy Fermi liquid (FL) phase of ℋKL\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL}. With the density of c�c_{\alpha} equal to 1+p1+p, the total density of the ‘large’ Fermi surface is 2+p2+p. As a trivial filled band with density 2 can always be removed, we obtain ‘small’ Fermi surface associated with density pp in the FL phase of ℋKL\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL}. So the total area of hole pockets is p/2p/2. While this is the Luttinger value for ℋKL\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL}, it is not for ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM}. The 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} have an effective ferromagnetic Kondo coupling to the conduction electrons c�c_{\alpha} (mediated by the antiferromagnetic J⟂J_{\perp} and the antiferromagnetic JKJ_{K}), and so we can expect them to decouple from the top two layers. Indeed, we obtain a FL* phase for ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM} if the 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} layer forms a spin liquid, and the effects of J⟂J_{\perp} in Eq. (178) can be treated perturbatively. This leads the identification in Fig. 29 of the FL* pseudogap metal with the combination of a Kondo lattice FL state of c�c_{\alpha} and 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1}, and a spin liquid of 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2}.

We can now summarize the FL* construction of the Hubbard model in the following simple terms. We express the Hubbard model as a theory of antiferromagnetic paramagnons, and then fractionalize the S=1S=1 paramagnon into two S=1/2S=1/2 spins, 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} and 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2}. The 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} spins form a Kondo lattice heavy Fermi liquid with the electrons c�c_{\alpha} to yield the hole pockets. The 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins form the spin liquid needed to satisfy the constraints in Section 7.1.

7.4 Mean field theory of the cuprate pseudogap.

We can now obtain a mean-field theory of the pseudogap by extending the Kondo lattice mean-field theory to the Hamiltonian ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM} in Eq. (178).

We begin with the top two layers of electrons c�c_{\alpha} and spins 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} in the ALM in Fig. 28. We proceed with parton decomposition of 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} in terms of the fermionic spinons f1​�f_{1\alpha} as in Eq. (95)

𝑺1​𝒊=12​f1​𝒊​�†​��​�​f1​𝒊​�,\displaystyle{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}=\frac{1}{2}f_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{1{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,, (179)

and obtain the mean-field fermion Kondo lattice Hamiltonian for the c�c_{\alpha} and f1​�f_{1\alpha}:

ℋKLmf=∑𝒊,𝒋[−t𝒊​𝒋​c𝒊​�†​c𝒋​�−t1,𝒊​𝒋​f1​𝒊​�†​f1​𝒋​�]−∑𝒊(�​c𝒊​�†​f1​𝒊​�+�∗​f1​𝒊​�†​c𝒊​�).\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}=\sum_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}}}\left[-t_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}c_{{\bm{j}}\alpha}-t_{1,{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}f^{\dagger}_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}f_{1{\bm{j}}\alpha}\right]-\sum_{{\bm{i}}}(\Phi\,c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}f_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}+\Phi^{\ast}\,f^{\dagger}_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha})\,. (180)

Here �\Phi is decoupling field of the JKJ_{K} exchange interaction in Eq. (178), and is illustrated in Fig. 35. At the mean-field level, we can assume the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid remains decoupled, and important effects of this spin liquid will be discussed in Section 7.6.

When considered as a theory of the Kondo lattice model ℋKL\mathcal{H}_{\rm KL}, the FL state corresponds to the condensation of the decoupling field �\Phi. On the other hand, on the Hilbert space of the full ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM}, this same �\Phi condensed phase is the FL* state. This interesting inversion is highlighted in Fig. 30: the single band model has an ‘inverted’ Kondo lattice transition.

The magnitude of �\Phi determines the value of the electronic gap in the anti-nodal region of the Brillouin zone (near momenta (�,0)(\pi,0), (0,�)(0,\pi)).

Fig 31 shows the electron spectral density (as measured by photoemission) at zero frequency for both the electron and hole pockets, computed by diagonalizing Eq. (180).

We can now present in Fig. 32 the close analogy between the FL* state obtained in the ALM and the state presented in Fig. 26 as highlighted in the box before the beginning of Section 7.3

A key observation is that the number of spin-singlet blue dimers in the ALM is exactly NN more than in the dimer model of Fig. 26, while the number of green dimers is the same. This is acceptable because NN spin singlets is precisely the number that can be accommodated in a trivial rung-singlet state of a bilayer antiferromagnet.

The connection in Fig. 32 shows that the ALM is, in a sense, ‘minimal’. For a FL* mean field theory with both a small Fermi surface and spinons, we need the middle and bottom ancilla layers to provide the vacancy-spin and singlet valence bonds respectively. And a bonus, not available in the quantum dimer analysis of Ref. [119, 162] or other approaches [156, 160, 161], is that it also provides a mean-field theory which captures the FL large Fermi when the bottom two layers are in a rung-singlet state.

7.5 Wavefunction for FL* and cold atom observations.

A separate mean-field approach is to work with variational wavefunctions. The ancilla layer method was the first to provide a variational wavefunction for the FL* phase of the single-band Hubbard model.

Here f1f_{1} is obtained from the parton decomposition of 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} in Eq. (179), and the Slater determinant of (c,f1)(c,f_{1}) is the ground state of ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf} in Eq. (180). Note that this wavefunction depends only upon the co-ordinates of the cc electrons alone, as the co-ordinates of the f,f1f,f_{1} fermions have been projected out. This wavefunction replaces the ‘vanilla’ Gutzwiller projected wavefunctions of the cc electrons alone [183] in the underdoped region. We see rather explicitly in Eq. (181) the expressivity of the layered construction [184], allowing us to include both a small Fermi surface and a spin liquid in the same state.

A summary of this wavefunction, and its connection to the cuprate phase diagram appear in Figs. 33 and 34.

Ref. [186] has given an appealing quantum information theoretic interpretation of the wavefunction in Eq. (181). We can view the projection into singlet pairs as a set of Bell-pair measurements of the ancilla spins. This measurement teleports the entanglement of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins to the cc electrons.

The wavefunction Eq. (181) has been studied numerically in Refs. [176, 177, 186], with the couplings in ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf} treated as variational parameters. One of the variational parameters is the hybridization/Higgs field �\Phi, which is non-zero in the FL* phase and decreases with increasing doping until it vanishes at a FL*-FL transition. The results of Refs. [176, 177] successfully capture the evolution of local, multi-point spin and charge correlations with doping as measured in cold atom experiments on the square lattice fermionic Hubbard model [175, 178, 187]. The results of Ref. [186] compare well with the exact diagonalization of Hubbard models in one and two dimensions.

7.6 SU(2) gauge theory of the onset of nodal dd-wave superconductivity from FL*

This section addresses the fate of the FL* pseudogap as the temperature is lowered, upon including the coupling to the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid in ℋpseudogap\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap} in Eq. (185). This Hamiltonian specifically choses the �\pi-flux spin liquid of Section 4 for the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layer. We will show that for this spin liquid there is a transition to a conventional BCS-type dd-wave superconductor, with anisotropic nodal velocities for the Boboliubov quasiparticles, and h/(2​e)h/(2e) vortices. Nevertheless the transition itself is not of the BCS type with a Cooper-pairing instability of a Fermi surface. Instead, the transition is driven by the confinement of the fractionalized excitations of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid. We also find nearby instabilities to charge ordering, consistent with observations—see the review in Ref. [188] for more information.

We note here recent numerics which support the idea of the dd-wave superconductor emerging from the doping-induced confinement of the �\pi-flux spin liquid. As we have discussed in Section 4, the �\pi-flux spin liquid is one description of the quantum-criticality between the Néel and VBS states. The numerical studies of Refs. [189, 190] examined the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice antiferromagnet near the Néel-VBS transition, and indeed found dd-wave superconductivity upon doping.

Now we return to the analysis of the pseudogap using the ALM in Eq. (178). In Section 7.4, we presented a mean field analysis in terms of decoupled Kondo lattice and spin liquid models. This section will couple them using the methods developed in Sections 3 and 6.

On the spin liquid layer of 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins we write a parton decomposition which parallels that in Eq. (95) and (179)

𝑺2​𝒊=12​f𝒊​�†​��​�​f𝒊​�.\displaystyle{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}=\frac{1}{2}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,. (182)

Then the analysis of the exchange interactions within the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layer is precisely that in Section 4. W decouple the J𝒊​𝒋J_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} term in Eq. (178) to ℋS​L​f\mathcal{H}_{SLf} in Eq. (4.1) realizing a �\pi-flux state of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins with a SU(2) gauge field.

To couple this spin liquid to the Kondo lattice, we have to decouple the J⟂J_{\perp} term coupling the f1f_{1} and ff spinons in Eq. (178). Given the SU(2) gauge structure of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layer, it pays to decouple the J⟂J_{\perp} term in a manner which keeps the SU(2) gauge invariance explicit. These Yukawa couplings are analogs of the green dot in Fig. 25.

We can now collect all terms to write down the complete Hamiltonian needed for our analysis of the pseudogap metal, and its low temperature instabilities.

ℋpseudogap=ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY+ℰ2​[B,U]+ℰ4​[B,U]\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap}=\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y}+\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U] (185)

specified in Eqs. (180), (4.1), (184), (161). This Hamiltonian has 3 fermions c�c_{\alpha}, f1​�f_{1\alpha}, f�f_{\alpha} whose transformations under SU(2) gauge, spin rotation, and electromagnetic charge symmetries are in Eqs. (154), (155), (156), with f1​�f_{1\alpha} transforming just like c�c_{\alpha}. As illustrated in Fig. 35, the Higgs boson �\Phi controls the hybridization between the electrons cc and the spinons f1f_{1} in the Kondo lattice formed by the top two layers, while the the Higgs boson BB couples the Kondo lattice to the spin liquid on the bottom layer, with SU(2) gauge field U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}. The energy symmetry considerations on BB are the same as at half-filling, and so the energy functionals ℰ2,4\mathcal{E}_{2,4} are the same as those at half-filling. The only difference from half-filling is the absence of particle-hole symmetry, and this allows linear time-derivative terms in the BB effective action, which will be generated from ℋY\mathcal{H}_{Y} [96].

It would be interesting to extend the variational computations, using the wavefunction in Eq. (181), of the metallic states [176, 177, 186] to the superconducting and charge-ordered states now permitted by the introduction of BB. Such a computation would start with the ground state of the fermions (c,f1,f)(c,f_{1},f) for the Hamiltonian ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y} (at Ui​j=1U_{ij}=1), project out the spin-singlets of the ancilla layers as in Eq. (181), and then use this projected wavefunction to optimize the energy of a Hubbard-type model. In addition to the variational parameters in ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}, such a computation would also optimize over an arbitrary spatial dependence of BB.

Finally, we note in passing that there is a remarkable similarity between Eq. (185), and the Weinberg-Salam theory of weak interactions [96]. Although the dispersions of the fermions and bosons have a lattice structure, the SU(2)×\times U(1) gauge structure (we treat the electromagnetic U(1) as global), and the Yukawa couplings between the Higgs and the fermions are similar, with the spinons mapping to neutrinos, and the electrons mapping to electrons.

7.7 Anisotropic velocities in the dd-wave superconductor

We now show how the problem of isotropic quasiparticle velocities (in contrast to observations in Ref. [18]), noted in Section 6, is resolved by the presence of the pocket Fermi surfaces described by ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf} in Eq. (180). The discussion below is based on the detailed computations presented in Refs. [191, 192].

Given the pocket Fermi surfaces and spinons in the FL* normal state, we imagine imposing a BCS type pairing on the Fermi surface excitations. If the pairing is dd-wave, it would lead to 8 nodal Bogoliubov points as shown in Fig. 36A. However this state also has the 4 nodal quasiparticles of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid, associated with the dispersion in Fig. 19. So strictly speaking, this state remains fractionalized, and is not a conventional dd-wave superconductor. It would be appropriate to call it d-SC*.

However, if we induce the pairing by the BB condensate in Eq. (184), the SU(2) gauge field is higgsed. Morever, the Yukawa coupling allows the nodal quasiparticles of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid to hybridize with the Bogoliubov quasiparticles of the pocket Fermi surfaces. The net result, sketched in Fig. 36B, is that the BB condensate can enable the nodal points on the ‘backsides’ of the pocket Fermi surfaces to mutually annihilate with the spinons of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid. We are then left with the 4 nodal quasiparticles on front sides of the pocket Fermi surfaces. The number of nodal points are the same as those obtained in conventional BCS theory from dd-wave pairing of a Fermi liquid. These remaining nodal points are associated with pairing on the pocket Fermi surfaces, and these is no reason for their velocity to be isotropic (unlike the spinons).

The annihilation of the extra nodal points occurs via hybridization between the electrons and spinons within a mean-field band structure of ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y} in Eqs. (180), (4), and (184) . Furthermore, computations which diagonalize this Hamiltonian with BB fixed and U=1U=1 do indeed yield anisotropic velocities similar to those observed. Unlike the situation in Section 6, the spinons do not become the Bogoliubov quasiparticles in the doped case; instead the spinons are needed to annihilate the extraneous Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

An interesting prediction can be made in the particular case of the electron-doped cuprates. In these materials, photoemission experiments have observed a normal state to superconductivity which is gapped near (�/2,�/2)(\pi/2,\pi/2) and has spectral weight only near electron pockets at the antinode [193]. If dd-wave superconductivity were to emerge as a BCS instability from such a normal state, the resulting superconductor should be gapped. However, the FL∗ theory yields a different prediction. Similar to how the spinon degrees of freedom emerge to annhilate with the backside pocket when BB Higgs condenses in the hole-doped case, the Dirac node of the spin liquid will appear with a finite spectral weight near (�/2,�/2)(\pi/2,\pi/2) when BB condenses, leading to a nodal superconductor. Such a prediction can be explored in future photoemission experiments in the electron doped cuprates [194] and could serve as an experimental test of the FL∗ theory.

8 The FL*-FL transition

There are two broad classes of theories for the hole-doped cuprate pseudogap in the literature. In the first class are theories in the ‘fluctuating order’ class, with thermal fluctuations between dd-wave superconductivity, charge and other orders [99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106]. The present FL* approach falls into the second class, with a novel, intrinsincally quantum ground state which builds in fermionic quantum entanglement of mobile electrons (to be contrasted with the bosonic quantum entanglement of insulating spin liquids). The existence of the FL* state sets up the possibility of a quantum phase transition from FL* to the conventional Fermi liquid (FL): a transition between two metals without any broken symmetry order parameter. Such an underlying FL*-FL transition has been argued [117] to be the key to understanding the cuprate phase diagram across optimal doping, as is reviewed in more detail elsewhere [188].

Fig. 37 (a similar figure is in Ref. [117]) shows the metallic phases as a function of the doping pp. Below a low p=psdwp=p_{\rm sdw} we have the AF Metal, which is distinguished from FL* by the presence of long-range antiferromagnetic order. Even so, the transition from the AF metal to FL* cannot be described in the Landau theory framework: the presence of a background spin liquid requires deconfined criticality with a fractionalized order parameter [195, 173].

At a larger p=pcp=p_{c}, we have the proposed transition between FL* and FL. A theory for this has been discussed elsewhere, and it involves a gauge theory with the Higgs field �\Phi [179, 196, 180]. This Higgs field �\Phi also appears as a variational parameter in the wavefunction for the FL* phase and its transition to the FL phase discussed in Section 7.5. Note that �\Phi is distinct from the Higgs field BB in Sections 6 and 7.6, as is illustrated in Fig. 35.

A key constraint satisfied by the theory is that the FL and FL* states have a transition at low temperatures to the same dd-wave superconductor, i.e. there is no transition within the superconducting state between over- and under-doping. In the over-doped regime, the transition from FL to the superconductor is described by the conventional BCS framework. In the under-doped regime, the transition from FL* to the same dd-wave superconductor is described by a confinement transition of a SU(2) gauge theory [96, 192, 82, 97, 98], employing the SU(2) gauge field of Section 4. But an important point is that the underlying FL*-FL transition is visible within the superconducting state in the differences in the vortex core structure [197, 98]. In the over-doped superconductor, the vortices exhibit [198] the Wang-MacDonald peak [199] obtained from a conventional BCS theory of a dd-wave superconductor; in the under-doped superconductor the underlying FL* normal state leads to [197, 98] modulations in the local density of states in the halo of the vortex core [200].

The underlying FL*-FL transition is also useful in developing a theory of the strange metal phase at higher temperatures, appearing in Figs. 33 and 34. In the presence of impurities, the strange metal has been argued [201, 202, 203, 204, 205] to be described by a two-dimensional extension of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model [206, 207].
